soil-form-140.title: Primary minerals, inherited unchanged from rock
soil-form-140.text: Much of a soil's grit was never made in the soil at all. Soil minerals come in two types. Primary minerals are found in soil but did not form there. They crystallized with their host igneous rock and have not been chemically altered since. By contrast, {{ref:soil-chem-235}} form as primary minerals weather. Primary mineral particles are mostly larger than 2 μm. They make up the silt, sand and gravel fractions. {{ref:soil-form-135}} supplies them: quartz, {{ref:soil-form-141}}, {{ref:soil-form-142}}, {{ref:soil-chem-226}}, {{ref:soil-form-144}}, amphibole, pyroxene and {{ref:soil-form-145}}. Silicates dominate the primary minerals in soil, and quartz and cristobalite are common soil tectosilicates, silicates built as a three-dimensional framework. The chain runs from primary rocks, the source of primary minerals, to the parent rocks those minerals compose.

soil-chem-186.title: Bowen's reaction series: the order in which magma freezes
soil-chem-186.text: Cool a basaltic magma slowly, and its minerals appear in a fixed order. The petrologist Norman L. Bowen worked out that order in the early 1900s. He melted powdered rock and noted which minerals formed as the temperature fell. Olivine and calcium plagioclase crystallize first. Pyroxene, amphibole and biotite follow, then sodium plagioclase, orthoclase, {{ref:soil-chem-226}} and finally quartz. This sequence of {{ref:soil-found-031}} is Bowen's reaction series. It has two branches. In the continuous branch, feldspars grow steadily richer in sodium as the melt cools. In the discontinuous branch, one mafic mineral, rich in iron and magnesium, gives way to the next. The order explains why some minerals tend to occur together in {{ref:soil-form-135}} and others almost never do. It also matters for soil. Minerals are most stable near the conditions where they formed, so the series ranks resistance to weathering at Earth's surface. Quartz, the last to form, lasts longest.

soil-chem-190.title: Infrared spectra that reveal water in minerals
soil-chem-190.text: Some minerals have no long-range order, yet still announce themselves. {{ref:soil-chem-097}} is one, identified by its distinctive infrared spectrum and its {{ref:soil-chem-228}} pattern. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy records how a solid, liquid or gas absorbs or emits infrared light over a wide range of wavelengths at once. A mathematical Fourier transform converts the raw data into the spectrum, which gives the method its name. Geologists use it to quantify water and carbon dioxide in minerals and glasses. With that X-ray method and electron diffraction, infrared spectroscopy is a standard way to study clays.

soil-chem-204.title: Coprecipitation: solids that drag dissolved metals down
soil-chem-204.text: A forming precipitate can carry down substances that would otherwise stay dissolved. That is coprecipitation. The captured material may sit inside the crystal lattice, be sealed in as the crystal grows, or cling to the precipitate's surface. {{ref:soil-fert-290}} too dilute to precipitate alone ride down with a carrier of similar crystal structure. The process matters in {{ref:soil-bio-059}}, in heavy metal transport, wastewater treatment and radionuclide migration around waste repositories. Wetlands built for treatment, the subject of {{ref:soil-water-260}}, remove phosphorus by coprecipitation with iron, aluminum and calcium compounds, and iron coagulants strip arsenic from water the same way.

soil-chem-208.title: Inner sphere complexes: ions that bond straight to minerals
soil-chem-208.text: Some ions hover near a mineral surface; others grab it. In an inner sphere complex, an ion binds directly to the surface with no water molecules between them. In an outer sphere complex, water keeps the two apart. Only ions with a high affinity for surface sites form the inner kind, including specifically adsorbed ions that bond covalently. Surface hydroxyl groups act as electron-donating ligands. On oxide surfaces the metal ion is a Lewis acid, an electron-pair acceptor, and the ligand a Lewis base, an electron-pair donor. Sorption of protonated ligands therefore depends on pH. These complexes govern how {{ref:soil-fert-290}} move or stay put in soil, where natural sorbents are often metal oxides. Sulfate held this way can slow or prevent the dissolution of iron and manganese oxides. Alkaline earth metals sorb less as their ions get larger, so they grow more mobile during weathering. Through such bonds, soil properties decide whether nutrients and pollutants are retained or lost.

soil-chem-238.title: How layered silicate minerals differ in charge and surface area
soil-chem-238.text: Layered silicate minerals of one family can differ enormously in how much they hold. Phyllosilicates differ mainly in {{ref:soil-chem-047}} capacity, CEC, and in reactive surface area, which depend on {{ref:soil-chem-085}} and on whether the interlayer admits cations. {{ref:soil-chem-088}} has little substitution and does not expand, so its CEC is 2-16 cmol(+) per kg and its surface is only external, 5-15 m2 per g. {{ref:soil-chem-094}} and chlorite have substantial substitution, but a tightly bound K+ or hydroxide interlayer blocks expansion, so CEC is limited: 20-40 for the first and 10-40 for chlorite. {{ref:soil-chem-091}} admits interlayer cations, giving CEC 60-120 and an internal surface of 570-660 m2 per g, and soils rich in it swell and shrink strongly. {{ref:soil-chem-095}} has CEC of 100-150 but expands little, because its charge, concentrated near the interlayer, binds cations tightly and restricts water entry. Fe/Al oxyhydroxides have CEC near 0-3 but 200-500 m2 per g of surface, and amorphous minerals of aluminum and silicon range from 5 to 350 CEC.

soil-env-321.title: How compaction stunts roots
soil-env-321.text: Compaction removes large pores and raises penetration resistance, restricting roots and the organisms that live in soil. The large pores between aggregates go first. That hurts fine and medium soils most, because they depend on those pores for infiltration, percolation and air exchange, while coarse soils suffer less. Compacted soil also hardens as it dries, since many small pores hold water under high suction. A good soil keeps penetration resistance below the 300 psi (2 MPa) level at which root growth ceases, but compacted soil quickly exceeds it. Growing roots need pores wider than about 0.1 mm, the size of most root tips. Without them roots stay short and thick, with few fine roots or root hairs, and take up water and nutrients poorly. Roots meeting a mechanical barrier also send a hormonal signal that slows shoot growth, an effect hard to separate from drought. {{ref:soil-env-320}} limits deep rooting and raises drought losses in rain-fed farming. Earthworms, insects and aerobic microbes need large pores and air exchange, so compacted soils hold fewer of them, though they return quickly once better practices are adopted. The process itself is described in {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-form-010.title: The B horizon, the soil's collecting zone
soil-form-010.text: Brown or reddish, the B horizon takes its color from {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, because it holds less organic matter than the A horizon above. It is a subsurface mineral horizon, formed below a horizon lettered A, E, H or O. Its original rock structure is largely gone, and {{ref:soil-form-155}} have altered or enriched its material. It is commonly called subsoil. Where it gathers material moving down from the A and E horizons, it is also called the illuvial horizon. Its marks include residual oxides or clay, lost carbonates or gypsum, and washed-in clay, iron, aluminum, organic material, carbonates, gypsum or silica. It generally has a structure or consistency that differs from the layers above and below. Gleying alone does not make a B horizon, nor do carbonates cut off from a genetic horizon above. The Australian system splits it into B1, transitional from A, B2, with concentrated clay or oxides, and B3, transitional to the C or D horizon.

soil-form-011.title: The C horizon, raw material soil barely touched
soil-form-011.text: Below the layers that {{ref:soil-form-155}} have reshaped lies material it has barely touched. The C horizon is that layer: anything above hard bedrock that those processes have little affected and that lacks the properties of O, A, E or B horizons. It includes sediments, saprolite and soft bedrock that a spade can dig when moist and that usually slakes, crumbling in water, within 24 hours. It forms in deposits such as loess, flood deposits and landslides, or by weathering of bedrock in place. Unless a change in parent material separates them, a break covered in {{ref:soil-form-015}}, it resembles the parent material of the soil above, though C material may differ. Plant roots can penetrate it, so it is an important growing medium. It may be enriched with carbonates and other soluble compounds washed down from above. Layers cemented by silica, carbonates or gypsum stay C unless those processes have clearly affected them; then they become B horizons.

soil-form-021.title: Topsoil, the thin living layer that feeds plants
soil-form-021.text: One inch (2.5 cm) of topsoil can take 500 to 1,000 years to form. The United States loses almost 3 tons of it per acre every year. Topsoil is the upper layer of soil, richest in {{ref:soil-found-045}} and microorganisms, where most of the soil's biological activity takes place. It is a mix of mineral particles and that matter, usually 5–10 inches (13–25 cm) deep. The water and air it holds encourage that activity. Roots concentrate here, because plants draw most of their nutrients from this layer. Bacteria and fungi break down organic material, while insects aerate and turn the soil. Its depth runs from the surface to the first densely packed layer, described in {{ref:soil-form-023}}. Classification systems label it as one of two horizons, covered in {{ref:soil-form-006}} and {{ref:soil-form-008}}. More of it helps its particles hold together. Dried-out topsoil loses much of its volume, and the wind carries it off more easily. The optimum {{ref:soil-fert-184}} for UK topsoil is less than 20:1. Today, use and erosion strip topsoil faster than new soil forms. Cover crops, {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, {{ref:soil-agri-099}} and windbreaks slow the loss and keep it fertile.

soil-form-023.title: Subsoil, where the rain drops its cargo
soil-form-023.text: Rain does more than wet the ground. It carries weathering products such as clay and the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} downward, dissolved or as fine suspended particles, and most of them settle in the subsoil. Subsoil is the layer beneath {{ref:soil-form-021}}, a mix of sand, silt and clay with much less {{ref:soil-found-045}}. With so little of it, the subsoil's color comes mainly from those iron minerals. Physical, chemical and biological activity cluster its particles into a definite arrangement, and that sets it apart from the barely altered substratum below. It is not sterile, but it holds few soil organisms compared with the rich layer above. Most soil mapping systems give it the letter B, with a substratum lettered C beneath; {{ref:soil-form-010}} and {{ref:soil-form-011}} return to both. Human activity has mixed topsoil and subsoil in many environments. Builders have used clay-rich subsoil for millennia, as adobe, cob, rammed earth and wattle and daub.

soil-form-028.title: Fragipans, brittle layers that still puzzle soil scientists
soil-form-028.text: A fragipan holds virtually no roots, yet its air-dry fragments fall apart in water. It is a diagnostic horizon of {{ref:soil-class-006}}: an altered, dense subsurface layer that blocks water and roots. Written Bx or Btx, it limits how the land can be used much as the layer in {{ref:soil-form-027}} does. It contains no calcium or magnesium carbonate and does not fizz in dilute HCl. Proposed origins include glacial compaction, frozen ground, physical ripening, inheritance from ancient buried soils, and hydroconsolidation, the collapse of structure under loading and wetting. Soil scientists still debate how fragipans form, how to define them and whether they exist in some landscapes.

soil-phys-099.title: Matric suction, the pull that holds damp soil together
soil-phys-099.text: Above the groundwater, soil water is under tension rather than pressure. Matric suction is that negative pore water pressure in unsaturated soil, caused by {{ref:soil-phys-260}} in the pores and defined as pore air pressure minus pore water pressure. Because the water pressure is negative, effective stress there is slightly greater than total stress. Capillary rise is inversely proportional to pore diameter, so sandy soils have much shallower capillary zones than clays and silts. Heavy rain soaking in lowers the suction, cutting the soil's shear strength and the stability of slopes. It is measured with the instrument described in {{ref:soil-water-221}}.

soil-phys-196.title: Retardation: why contaminants lag behind the water
soil-phys-196.text: A contaminant does not always travel at the speed of the water that carries it. Retardation by {{ref:soil-chem-145}} is the slowing of a contaminant's average movement relative to groundwater because it sticks to soil surfaces, measured by a retardation factor. This holds the contaminant back until the amount set by the equilibrium has been taken up. The factor depends on the chemistry of both the contaminant and the aquifer, and it is analogous to the retardation factor of chromatography. Less soluble contaminants can move hundreds or thousands of times slower than water, so only the more soluble species travel far. This differs from the spreading described in {{ref:soil-phys-192}} and {{ref:soil-phys-193}}. Unlike the slow drift of molecules and dispersion, which merely spread a contaminant, retardation changes its global average velocity, so it can be much slower than the water. Chromatography gives the clearest definition. There the retardation factor R is the fraction of the substance in the mobile phase at equilibrium: the quantity in the mobile phase divided by the total quantity in the system. In planar chromatography, RF is the substance's travel distance over the solvent front's. It always lies between 0 and 1, because nothing outruns the solvent. A spot that travels 2.5 cm while the solvent front travels 5.0 cm gives 0.50.

soil-phys-197.title: One equation for drifting and spreading
soil-phys-197.text: Most soil models describe salt on the move with one equation. The scalar transport equation, which extends {{ref:soil-phys-241}} with a flow term, tracks a quantity moved by both {{ref:soil-phys-240}} and {{ref:soil-phys-193}}. It is a parabolic partial differential equation built on the continuity equation, which keeps account of what enters and leaves. Diffusive flux comes from {{ref:soil-phys-181}} as −D∇c; advective flux is vc. A source or sink term R adds or removes the quantity, as when a chemical reaction creates or destroys a species. In porous media, v is the superficial velocity. SWAP, DrainMod-S, UnSatChem and Hydrus all couple the {{ref:soil-water-238}} with it, moving salts by advection and dispersion.

soil-phys-213.title: Transpiration: how plants lift soil water into the air
soil-phys-213.text: An acre of corn gives off about 3,000–4,000 U.S. gallons (11,000–15,000 liters) of water a day. That flow is transpiration: water moving through a plant and evaporating from its leaves, stems and flowers. It is passive and costs the plant no energy. It also cools the plant and drives the mass flow of {{ref:soil-fert-289}}. Very little of the water roots take up goes into growth; 97–99.5% is lost by transpiration and guttation. Two stretches set the pace. From soil to root, flow depends on the soil's hydraulic conductivity and the pressure gradient through the soil. Up the plant, water moves mainly down differences in water potential. When roots take up less than leaves lose, stomata close. That slows nutrient uptake and limits {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and growth. The soil's temperature and moisture influence how far stomata open, and roots struggle in dry, very fertile or salty soils. Isotope measurements show transpiration is the larger part of evapotranspiration. They also show transpired water differs from {{ref:soil-phys-203}} and streams, so soil water is less well mixed than assumed. It is measured with potometers, {{ref:soil-water-248}}, porometers, plant gas-exchange systems and sap flow sensors.

soil-phys-240.title: Diffusion: spreading over short distances
soil-phys-240.text: Diffusion does its work over tiny distances. Under normal conditions {{ref:soil-phys-243}} dominates only over lengths from nanometers to millimeters; beyond that, convection takes over. It is the net movement of atoms, ions, molecules or energy from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration. A gradient in chemical potential drives it, which sets it apart from bulk flow, where a whole body of material moves down a pressure gradient. {{ref:soil-phys-181}} puts numbers on it. The diffusive flux is proportional to the negative concentration gradient, with the diffusion coefficient D as the constant. In a porous medium such as soil, the porosity must be counted in both the flux and accumulation terms. As porosity goes to zero, the molar flux for a given concentration gradient goes to zero too.

soil-water-003.title: How rain and runoff carry soil away
soil-water-003.text: Almost 36 billion tons of soil are lost to water every year, according to a global model. Water erosion is the removal of soil by rainfall and by the surface runoff it produces, a form of {{ref:soil-water-001}}. It begins with the rain itself. Raindrops bombard aggregates and detach small particles that are easily transported, by splash or by water running downhill, to a low area where they are deposited. Runoff, the flow described in {{ref:soil-water-019}}, begins when the soil is saturated or when rain falls faster than water can infiltrate (see {{ref:soil-water-180}}). Runoff with enough flow energy carries loosened soil particles down the slope as sediment. Rain and runoff cause four main types of erosion, in rising severity: splash, sheet, {{ref:soil-water-025}} and {{ref:soil-water-027}}. Concentrated runoff cuts small channels called rills. If runoff keeps deepening them, they may grow into gullies, a gully being a rill too deep for tillage equipment to smooth. {{ref:soil-water-005}} and rilling cause most soil erosion. The damage is not evenly spread, either. Water erosion removes soil mainly from the middle and lower parts of a slope rather than from hilltops.

soil-water-156.title: Saturated and unsaturated flow: pushed by gravity, pulled by suction
soil-water-156.text: Water in soil moves in two quite different ways, and the line between them sits at {{ref:soil-water-177}}. Between 0 and 33 kPa suction, up to that point, gravity and differences in water pressure push water away from where it was applied. That is saturated flow. At higher suctions the push gives way to a pull. Water's {{ref:soil-phys-253}} to soil solids sets up a suction gradient, which draws water from wetter to drier soil and from macropores to micropores. That is unsaturated flow. The lab manual states the same split in other units: saturated flow at tensions of 0 to -0.3 bar, driven by hydrostatic head, and unsaturated flow at 0.3 to 31 bars, driven by a tension gradient. ({{ref:soil-water-172}} explains these suctions.) Unsaturated flow is slow, at most about 2.5 cm a day, so roots keep dying back and growing toward moister soil. It slows because the connected wet pathways shrink as soil dries. {{ref:soil-water-193}} therefore depends on water content, and it falls in a very non-linear way as soil dries. Six factors control infiltration and movement: texture, structure, organic matter, depth to impervious layers such as hardpans or bedrock, water already present, and {{ref:soil-phys-137}}. Warm soils take in water faster, while frozen soils, including {{ref:soil-env-129}}, may not absorb it at all, depending on how they froze. {{ref:soil-water-238}} gives the rate of change of moisture in unsaturated soil. Lewis Richardson first published it in 1922, and software such as Hydrus solves it numerically.

soil-water-172.title: Water potential: why water flows from soil to sky
soil-water-172.text: Water climbs from soil into roots, up a stem, out through the leaves and into the air without any pump. Each step has a more negative water potential than the one before, so the water flows passively. Water potential is the potential energy of water per unit volume, compared with pure water under reference conditions. In soils the reference is usually pure water at the soil surface. Written with the Greek letter ψ, it expresses water's tendency to move because of {{ref:soil-phys-258}}, gravity, mechanical pressure and matrix effects such as {{ref:soil-phys-252}}. Unrestricted water moves from higher to lower potential. Dissolved solutes lower the potential; added pressure raises it. In soil, total potential sums three parts: {{ref:soil-water-173}} from this effect, an osmotic part in saline soil and a gravitational part that drives downward flow. A saturated soil sits at 0 kPa. After free drainage, at {{ref:soil-water-177}}, it is −33 kPa, and at the {{ref:soil-water-178}} −1500 kPa. Dry air is typically about −100 MPa. No single instrument covers the whole range. Electrical resistance blocks read from −90 to −1500 kPa, while {{ref:soil-water-223}} reaches −10,000 kPa.

soil-water-173.title: Matric potential: the grip of grains on water
soil-water-173.text: Water held in an unsaturated soil always has less energy than pure water, because the soil's solids hold on to it. That hold is matric potential, the part of water potential that comes from water's attraction to solid particles and the curved menisci it forms between them. Water's {{ref:soil-phys-253}} to solids, with cohesion among water molecules, creates {{ref:soil-phys-260}}, and force is needed to break it, as {{ref:soil-phys-095}} showed. Its size depends on the spacing between particles, which sets meniscus width, and on the chemistry of the solids. Matric potential is always negative and occurs only in unsaturated soil above the water table. Near zero, nearly all pores are full. Water draining into less moist soil of similar porosity is generally at −10 to −30 kPa. It is often large compared with the other components, and though the flow it drives may be slow, it is vital for supplying water to roots.

soil-water-175.title: The water retention curve, a soil's moisture signature
soil-water-175.text: In 1907 Edgar Buckingham filled soil columns 48 inches tall with six soils, from sand to clay, and drew the first water retention curve. The curve links a soil's water content to its {{ref:soil-water-172}}. Also called the soil moisture characteristic, it differs between soil types and predicts water storage, plant water supply and aggregate stability. Near zero potential the soil is almost saturated and holds water mainly by capillarity. As it dries, the remaining water is bound ever more strongly, in the smallest pores, at grain contacts and as adsorbed films. Sandy soils release most of their water at higher potentials. Clayey soils, which also bind water through {{ref:soil-phys-253}} and {{ref:soil-phys-258}}, release it only at lower ones. At any given potential, peaty soils usually hold far more water than clayey soils, and clayey soils more than sandy ones. Even one soil has two curves. Pores fill and drain differently, so hysteresis, a lag between wetting and drying, gives separate wetting and drying curves.

soil-water-234.title: Deciding when to water, and for how long
soil-water-234.text: Up to 50% of landscape water is wasted by inefficient methods, the EPA WaterSense program estimates. Irrigation scheduling is how managers decide how often and for how long to water. The aim is to wet the whole root zone while minimizing overwatering and keeping water use efficiency high. Refilling depleted water before stress sets in avoids moisture stress. Methods range from watching plants for wilting and judging soil by feel, through sensors in the root zone, to {{ref:soil-water-235}}. Root-zone sensors include capacitance sensors, neutron probes for accurate deep readings, and the {{ref:soil-water-221}}. Scheduling has moved from calendar timers to smart controllers that respond to weather-based {{ref:soil-water-161}} or to measured soil moisture. Soil-based controllers either skip a timed cycle when the soil is wet or start watering only when moisture falls to a set threshold. Good scheduling prevents root rot and drought stress, and daily soil moisture estimates cut the risk of runoff and erosion.

soil-water-239.title: A sturdier way to simulate unsaturated flow
soil-water-239.text: Where Richards solvers can fail, this method is guaranteed to converge. The finite water-content vadose zone flow method is a one-dimensional alternative to solving Richards' equation numerically. It solves the advection-like term of the {{ref:soil-water-206}} as three ordinary differential equations, for infiltrating water, falling slugs and capillary groundwater. Being explicit, it is cheap to solve and mass-conserving, and it handles the sharp wetting fronts that Richards solvers struggle with. It assumes soil homogeneous in layers and omits {{ref:soil-phys-240}} of soil water, which barely affects flux accuracy. It works with any monotonic retention and conductivity relations, such as Brooks and Corey or van Genuchten–Mualem.

soil-form-014.title: Horizon suffixes, small letters with big meanings
soil-form-014.text: One lowercase letter can say what happened in a layer. Horizon suffixes are added to a master symbol to record particular features or {{ref:soil-form-155}}. In the USDA field book, t marks illuvial silicate clay, k pedogenic calcium carbonate, g strong gleying and p a plow layer. Others include b for a buried genetic horizon, f for permanently frozen ground, x for {{ref:soil-form-028}} features and y for gypsum. WRB letters borrow from other languages: k from German Karbonat, t from German Ton, clay, n from natrium and z from Dutch zout, salt. Suffixes combine in order of dominance, as in Btng or Btgb.

soil-water-163.title: Soil suction and pF: a scale for how hard water clings
soil-water-163.text: Oven-dry soil grips its last water with a suction of 1,000,000 kPa. Soil suction is the negative of soil water potential, the force needed to pull water out of soil. Water stays where its {{ref:soil-phys-253}} to soil particles beats the cohesion between water molecules, and that hold sets its availability to plants. The pF scale is the common logarithm of suction in centimeters of water, so pF 3 equals 1000 cm, 98 kPa or 0.98 bar. As roots thin a water film, suction rises to 1500 kPa (pF 4.2), the wilting point. Air-dry soil sits at 100,000 kPa (pF 6), oven-dry soil at pF 7.

soil-phys-259.title: The water molecule and what makes it unusual
soil-phys-259.text: Almost everything water does in soil starts with the shape of one molecule. Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom in a bent, polar molecule. It can make up to four hydrogen bonds, which explains its unusual thermodynamic properties. Cohesion and {{ref:soil-phys-253}} give high {{ref:soil-phys-260}}, 71.99 mN/m at 25 degrees C, and {{ref:soil-phys-252}} that lifts water over 100 m in trees. Specific heat, the energy needed to warm it, is very high at 4184 J/(kg K) at 20 degrees C, with a heat of vaporization of 40.65 kJ/mol. Density peaks at 3.98 degrees C, so between 0 and 3.98 degrees C water shows an unusual negative thermal expansion. Its high dielectric constant makes water an excellent solvent for hydrophilic substances, but not hydrophobic ones. Over long periods it weathers and erodes rock into soil and sediment.

soil-phys-193.title: Advection, the river that carries what it holds
soil-phys-193.text: Dump ink into a river and it travels downstream as a pulse. The river's own current carries it, and that carrying has a name: advection, the transport of a substance or quantity by the bulk motion of a fluid. It needs currents, so it cannot happen in rigid solids. It also excludes the slow drift of molecules on their own, called {{ref:soil-phys-240}}. The ink does both at once, riding the current while it spreads, and the sum of the two is convection. Underground the same thing happens in {{ref:soil-phys-203}}. There advection carries contaminants along the main direction of flow at the seepage velocity, the speed at which water actually moves through the pores. Physicists write it as the advection equation, a first-order hyperbolic partial differential equation. It comes from a conservation law: whatever is transported is neither created nor lost along the way.

soil-phys-192.title: How pollution travels with moving groundwater
soil-phys-192.text: A spill on the surface can turn up years later in a distant well. Contaminant transport in groundwater is the movement of dissolved contaminants with the water flowing underground, and contaminant hydrogeology is the field that studies it, a branch of {{ref:soil-phys-208}}. Some contaminants are man-made, such as petroleum products, nitrate or radionuclides. Others are natural, such as arsenic or salinity. Three main mechanisms move them. {{ref:soil-phys-193}} carries them at seepage velocity. {{ref:soil-phys-240}} spreads them from high to low concentration. Dispersion, covered in {{ref:soil-phys-194}}, spreads them further still. Those two only spread a contaminant, though. Sticking to the soil, the process of {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, does something different: it slows the contaminant's average velocity. Precipitation and decay also change what arrives. So the properties of the {{ref:soil-phys-201}}, beyond the flow itself, shape where pollution goes. Polluted groundwater forms a plume, and its advancing edge can reach wells and springs. Hydrologists track it with transport and groundwater models.

soil-found-121.title: Spheroidal weathering, peeling rock like an onion
soil-found-121.text: Square blocks of rock can rot into round boulders. Spheroidal, or onion-skin, weathering is the chemical attack on jointed bedrock that leaves concentric shells of decayed rock inside {{ref:soil-form-100}}. Water enters along the joints. Each block therefore weathers inward fastest at its corners, then its edges, then its faces, leaving a rounded core. These corestones, or woolsacks, stand as freestanding boulders or tors once erosion strips away the rotten rock around them. The alteration forms {{ref:soil-chem-235}} such as {{ref:soil-chem-088}} and {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, and swells the rock's volume. It has often been wrongly blamed on physical weathering alone, yet much of it happened in past humid, even tropical, climates.

soil-chem-135.title: Mica, the mineral that peels into thin elastic sheets
soil-chem-135.text: Mica comes apart in thin plates that bend and spring back. That property, perfect basal cleavage, defines the group: sheet silicate minerals whose crystals split easily along flat planes. They belong to the {{ref:soil-found-033}}, and the group holds 37 of them. {{ref:soil-chem-226}} and the biotite series are common examples. Each layer is a sandwich, a pattern called TOT-c. Two tetrahedral sheets are bonded to one octahedral sheet between them. Only interlayer cations, positively charged ions, hold the layers together, and weakly, hence the cleavage. In most micas aluminium replaces one in four silicon ions. That swap leaves each layer with a negative charge, which interlayer sodium, potassium or calcium ions neutralize. Dioctahedral micas have a gibbsite-like aluminium sheet. Trioctahedral ones have a brucite-like sheet of magnesium or ferrous iron. Mica is common in igneous and metamorphic rocks and appears as small flakes in some sedimentary rocks. Very fine-grained, variable 'clay micas' include {{ref:soil-chem-094}}, which is short of potassium between its layers. Weathering turns that mineral into this clay and, together with feldspars, into kaolin minerals such as dickite.

soil-chem-079.title: Clay minerals, the sheet silicates born of water
soil-chem-079.text: For a long time clay looked like ordinary rock ground very fine. Only with {{ref:soil-chem-228}} in the 1930s did it prove to be mainly sheet silicates formed as secondary minerals, not tiny grains of quartz, feldspar or mica. A clay mineral is a hydrous aluminium phyllosilicate: a silicate built in sheets that may also carry iron, magnesium, alkali metals and other cations. Its structure rests on flat hexagonal sheets like those of the mica minerals. Water is essential. Clay minerals form in its presence, as common products of {{ref:soil-found-052}}, including the weathering of feldspar, and of low-temperature hydrothermal alteration. That need for water makes them rare in the Solar System, though they have been detected on Mars, Ceres and other bodies. On Earth they are very common in soils and in fine-grained rocks such as shale, mudstone, siltstone, slate and phyllite. In a soil they never stop forming. For as long as the soil exists, new clay arises by inheritance, by neoformation or by transformation of earlier minerals. Most soil clays are crystalline, but some are amorphous. A soil's clay is a mixture of types, often with one dominating according to the kind of soil. The charges on clay minerals matter for crops. With {{ref:soil-found-045}}, they supply most of a soil's {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, its power to hold cations that plants feed on, such as potassium and ammonium.

soil-phys-250.title: The breakthrough curve: watching a solute emerge from a column
soil-phys-250.text: Feed a solute into one end of a column of porous material and measure what comes out of the other. The result is the breakthrough curve: the course of the solute's concentration at the outlet after a step change in inlet concentration. A fixed bed is purged with a carrier, then the adsorptive is added so that inlet concentration changes in a step, and the outlet concentration is monitored. Chromatography instead uses pulses. Integrating the area above the whole curve gives the material's maximum loading, and the time until the outlet reaches a threshold concentration gives its usable capacity to take up the solute. The curve's shape carries information on mass-transfer properties, which can be found by fitting simplified models to the data. It shows {{ref:soil-chem-145}} of the kind described in {{ref:soil-phys-196}} at work. The source page frames this in terms of engineering the process; it does not describe the soil-column version.

soil-form-008.title: The A horizon, where life and minerals mix
soil-form-008.text: Earthworms, potworms, arthropods, {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, fungi, bacteria and archaea crowd around plant roots in the A horizon, which is why some call it the biomantle. It is the uppermost mineral horizon, at the surface or below an O horizon, where humified {{ref:soil-found-045}} is intimately mixed with mineral material. Often called topsoil, it holds dark, decomposed matter of that kind. Burrowing animals stir it into the mineral matter, a mixing described in {{ref:soil-bio-047}}. The original rock structure is fully or largely gone. Biological activity reaches much deeper, though, so it cannot be the chief test, and A horizons are defined mostly relative to the layers beneath. Layers changed by plowing or pasturing count as A horizons, and the suffix p marks plowed ones. The Australian system divides it into A1, dark and most biologically active, A2, paler, and A3, a transition to the layer below.

soil-form-009.title: The E horizon, a pale layer washed clean
soil-form-009.text: Old, well-developed soils often hide a band paler than the layers around it. That is the E horizon, E for eluviated. It is a mineral horizon that has lost clay, iron, aluminum, organic material or a mix of these, leaving a concentration of sand and silt, mostly quartz. Where eluviation is pronounced, it appears below the A horizon and above a layer lettered B, covered in {{ref:soil-form-010}}. It differs from that lower layer by higher color value or lower chroma, coarser texture, or both. Sometimes it takes the color of its own sand and silt. The lost substances first had to form or collect in place, so an E horizon marks an advanced stage of soil development. In gravelly soils, burrowing animals commonly leave a stone layer near its base. The Australian system does not use E; it labels such washed-out layers A or B with the suffix e.

soil-bio-251.title: Mutualism, the partnerships where both sides win
soil-bio-251.text: About 80% of land plant species rely on fungi for inorganic compounds and {{ref:soil-fert-290}}, through {{ref:soil-bio-157}}. The plants pay in carbohydrates, a "biological barter." This is mutualism, an interaction between two or more species in which each gains a net benefit. Partnerships with these fungi are linked to the colonization of land by plants. {{ref:soil-bio-178}} fix nitrogen for legumes in return for carbohydrates. In Three Sisters farming, beans fix nitrogen in the soil for the corn they climb. Mutualism can also unravel. Plant lineages in nutrient-rich places have abandoned their fungal partners many times, and those fungi can turn parasitic on weak or dying plants.

soil-phys-210.title: The water budget: every drop accounted for
soil-phys-210.text: A basin, a field or a city can keep a water budget. A water balance states that the inflows to any water system equal its outflows plus the change in storage over a time interval. The system can be a soil column, a drainage basin, an irrigation area or a city. For a basin, P = Q + ET + ΔS: precipitation equals streamflow plus evapotranspiration plus the change in storage in soil or {{ref:soil-phys-203}}. The balance rests on conservation of mass and assumes a closed system, so water leaving for another basin must be accounted for. Comparing budgets across areas shows how geology, soils, vegetation and the way land is used affect the water cycle. The balance guides irrigation, runoff assessment, flood and pollution control, and the design of subsurface drainage by pipes, tile drains, ditches or wells. Monthly water balance models have been studied since the 1940s.

soil-chem-113.title: Redox: the electron trade behind rust and breath
soil-chem-113.text: A rusting nail and a breathing animal run the same kind of chemistry. Redox, short for reduction–oxidation, is any reaction in which the reactants' electron bookkeeping, set out in {{ref:soil-chem-178}}, changes. Oxidation is a loss of electrons, or a rise in that bookkeeping number. Reduction is a gain of electrons, or a fall in it. The two always happen together. Neither can occur on its own. When iron rusts, the iron is oxidized to an oxide, while oxygen is reduced by taking up the electrons the iron releases. The same trade powers respiration, {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, combustion and the corrosion of metals. The words are older than the idea of the electron. Oxidation first meant reacting with oxygen. Reduction meant the weight lost when ore is heated to extract its metal. Both were later widened to mean electron transfer. The word redox itself first appeared in a 1928 article by Leonor Michaelis and Louis B. Flexner. In soils, sediments and water, redox differs from place to place. Those differences drive the cycling of elements through living things and their surroundings, as {{ref:soil-chem-121}} shows.

soil-form-031.title: Cambic horizons, the first signs of change below ground
soil-form-031.text: The cambic horizon is the diagnostic horizon of last resort. It is a subsurface horizon showing early change by {{ref:soil-form-155}}, recognized when it does not meet the requirements of any other diagnostic horizon. It lacks appreciable illuviated clay, organic carbon, iron and aluminum oxyhydroxides, carbonate, gypsum or soluble salts. Its texture must be no coarser than loamy fine sand or very fine sand. It is commonest in {{ref:soil-class-101}} and {{ref:soil-class-100}}, also occurs in {{ref:soil-class-092}} and is written Bw or Bg. Along a {{ref:soil-form-063}}, it gains clay and develops into a clay-enriched Bt horizon once the soil becomes one of the {{ref:soil-class-090}} kind.

soil-phys-195.title: Molecular diffusion, fast over millimeters, slow over meters
soil-phys-195.text: Double the distance and it takes four times as long. The random thermal movement of molecules ({{ref:soil-phys-243}}) carries solutes from high to low concentration in the {{ref:soil-found-079}}. Over small distances it matters, but it spreads solutes slowly over large ones. Its coefficient is small and often negligible, except where groundwater barely moves, as in clay aquitards. This drift is a real physical process. Dispersion is an empirical factor that merely shares its mathematical form.

soil-form-155.title: Four ways soils gain, lose, change and move material
soil-form-155.text: What makes soil different from a layer of sediment? Four groups of processes, through which the {{ref:soil-form-043}} work: additions, losses, transformations and translocations. How far they have gone helps tell soils apart. Additions include organic matter, fertilizers, dust and other mineral soil arriving. Losses are soil moved away by wind or water, or chemical compounds leached, eroded or harvested. Transformations are the chemical or physical weathering of particles or components. Weathering releases ions from minerals or turns them into {{ref:soil-chem-235}}, which may reform deeper in the soil; ions lost altogether are leached. Translocations are movements of organic or mineral components between horizons. Eluviation removes material from a horizon and illuviation deposits it; clay, and iron and aluminium organic complexes, move down with soil water. Mixing, or turbation, is also a transfer, caused by organisms or by physical agents such as clay shrink-swell and freeze-thaw.

soil-chem-094.title: Illite, the potassium clay that will not swell
soil-chem-094.text: Illite is the only clay mineral that contains potassium, and that potassium shapes its character. Also called hydromica, it is a group of closely related, non-expanding 2:1 clay minerals, structurally close to the mica {{ref:soil-chem-226}}. Poorly hydrated potassium ions fill the space between its layers and bind them strongly, so illite does not swell. Those bonds also shrink its active surface. What little swelling it shows depends on how far potassium feldspar has weathered. Its {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, typically 20–30 meq/100 g, is higher than kaolinite's but lower than that of {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. Illite forms by alteration of that mica and feldspar in weathering and hydrothermal settings, and from swelling clays exposed to potassium-rich groundwater. It is common in sediments, soils and argillaceous rocks, and its share of soil clay rises relative to kaolinite toward cooler climates. It was first described in 1937 from the Maquoketa shale of Calhoun County, Illinois, and named after the state.

soil-chem-082.title: Telling one clay from another in the laboratory
soil-chem-082.text: Clay minerals are usually too fine for ordinary optical study. {{ref:soil-chem-228}} is the main tool for identifying them, aided by electron diffraction, spectroscopy and SEM-EDS. To put numbers on a soil's clays, analysts first measure its {{ref:soil-found-045}}, carbonates, free oxides and non-clay minerals. They then estimate clay percentages from how much glycol a sample takes up, {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, K2O and thermal data. This glycol test, a case of {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, measures how much ethylene glycol enters a clay's interlayer sites over eight hours of exposure to the vapor at 60 °C. Illite is estimated from its potassium oxide content, since it is the only clay mineral containing potassium.

soil-chem-227.title: Van der Waals force, the weak pull that adds up
soil-chem-227.text: No single van der Waals contact is strong, yet fine powders clump because of them. The force is a weak, distance-dependent attraction between atoms or molecules that is not a chemical bond. It begins with a transient shift in electron density that creates a short-lived charge, which a nearby atom is attracted to or repelled by. The force is repulsive at very short range, zero at an equilibrium distance of 0.3 to 0.5 nm for single atoms, and attractive beyond it. Past 1.0 nm it falls off roughly as the 7th power of distance. Three parts combine: London dispersion forces, Debye forces between permanent and induced dipoles, and Keesom forces between permanent dipoles. Induction and dispersion always attract, while the electrostatic part can attract or repel depending on orientation. Strength rises with polarizability. Pairwise energy is 0.06 kJ/mol between H atoms in H2, 0.44 kJ/mol between O atoms in O2, and 2.35 kJ/mol between xenon atoms. The forces are additive, cannot be saturated and have no directional character, so many weak contacts can add up to strong attraction. For very small particles, such as fine dry powders, the attraction beats gravity and drag, so the powders are cohesive. Free flow generally needs particles larger than about 250 micrometres. In soils, organic contaminants can be held in organic matter by weak van der Waals interactions, and physisorption is the weak van der Waals form of {{ref:soil-chem-145}}. Small particles of the kind met in a {{ref:soil-chem-154}} are where this matters most.

soil-form-032.title: Illuviation: where washed-down material comes to rest
soil-form-032.text: Everything water carries out of an upper layer has to stop somewhere. Illuviation is that stopping: the deposition in a lower layer of material, called illuvium, washed down by rainwater from a layer above. It is the matching half of eluviation. Illuvium includes {{ref:soil-found-045}}, silicate clay and the iron and aluminum compounds of {{ref:soil-chem-162}}. These collect in subsoil horizons lettered B, the zones of illuviation, described in {{ref:soil-form-010}}. The movement is basically vertical, unlike alluviation, the sideways transfer by running water. It works in two ways. In mechanical illuviation, a drier horizon draws water from percolating suspensions by capillarity, the pull of water into fine pores. Fine coatings are left along the channels, the subject of {{ref:soil-found-068}}. In chemical illuviation, dissolved constituents carried down by percolating water are deposited where the chemistry of the soil changes, especially its pH and its {{ref:soil-chem-123}}. Clay skins are called argillans, and horizons with enough washed-in clay are the ones named in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. In medium-textured soils, clay is often washed down the profile and gathers in the subsoil.

soil-class-157.title: Constructed soil, built to bring dead ground back
soil-class-157.text: A spent mine or a capped landfill has no usable topsoil left. Constructed soil fills that gap: a designed mixture of organic and mineral materials, often including repurposed organic waste, made to approximate natural soil and grow plants. Such soils are classed as {{ref:soil-class-145}}. They beat imported {{ref:soil-form-021}}, because harvesting topsoil degrades a second site and usually costs more. A mineral fraction sets texture, an organic fraction supplies nutrients, and a slowly decomposing carbon source, such as wood chips or {{ref:soil-fert-050}}, lasts longer. Organic matter in the top layer should not exceed 15% by weight, or the soil settles and waterlogs. A {{ref:soil-fert-184}} near 20:1 releases nutrients steadily. Layers thicker than about 45 cm can mimic natural {{ref:soil-found-001}} layers, with a sand or gravel drainage layer. Abrupt changes between layers decide whether water flows sideways or down, and where it perches. Living organisms and stable structure come later, as plants return. Every batch must meet legal limits for pathogens, harmful {{ref:soil-fert-290}}, salinity and pH.

soil-bio-102.title: How humus forms shift with forests, farms and climate
soil-bio-102.text: A site's humus form is not fixed. It shifts with vegetation, {{ref:soil-agri-221}}, pollution and climate. During forest succession organic horizons thicken, from mull in early stages towards moder under mature stands; in old natural forests the two alternate. Converting conifer forest to broadleaf turns moder into mull, and conifer plantations on deciduous land do the reverse. Farming that encourages earthworms can create a mull-like form called agri-mull. Pollution that harms earthworms slows decomposition and pushes the form towards mor, so humus forms offer a cheap early warning of contamination. Warmth favors mull, yet it also speeds microbial decomposition, depleting humus and leaving many soils with a negative carbon balance. A 3 °C rise in alpine grasslands reduced soil humus content. Earthworms disperse slowly, so change can lag, and adding them to turn moder into mull has given mixed results.

soil-chem-119.title: Breathing and photosynthesis as electron transfers
soil-chem-119.text: Every breath is a redox reaction. Aerobic respiration oxidizes fuels such as glucose and reduces oxygen to water. {{ref:soil-hist-147}} does roughly the opposite: it reduces carbon dioxide to sugars and oxidizes water to oxygen. It complements respiration, yet it is not simply its reverse. Living things often store and release energy through such reactions, relying on the steady cycling of the carriers NAD+ and NADH.

soil-form-019.title: Albic horizons, bleached layers below the surface
soil-form-019.text: Bleached and pale, the albic horizon is what remains when {{ref:soil-form-155}} move clay and oxides downward. It is a light-colored subsurface diagnostic horizon in both the WRB and {{ref:soil-class-006}}. {{ref:soil-class-099}}, acidic soils common in coniferous and boreal forests, usually have one. In {{ref:soil-class-147}} soils it tongues down into a clay-rich Bt horizon. In {{ref:soil-class-144}}, the topsoil can be completely bleached. {{ref:soil-class-137}} often show eluviation as an albic horizon beneath an umbric surface layer.

soil-phys-251.title: The Péclet number: advection against diffusion
soil-phys-251.text: Two kinds of transport compete in any moving fluid, and the Péclet number says which one wins. It is a dimensionless number giving the ratio of advective to diffusive transport rate, the two processes of {{ref:soil-phys-193}} and {{ref:soil-phys-195}}. For mass transfer, Pe = L u / D, with L a characteristic length, u flow velocity and D the {{ref:soil-phys-240}} coefficient; it equals the Reynolds number times the Schmidt number. It can also be written as the ratio of that spreading time to advection time. Where Pe is much greater than 1, advection predominates in mass transport because it takes much longer.

soil-form-022.title: Topsoil by the truckload
soil-form-022.text: Topsoil is also a product. Commercial topsoil is any soil mixture sold as topsoil: natural topsoil mined and conditioned for use, or a blend manufactured from minerals, {{ref:soil-fert-045}}, compost or paper mill sludge. Buyers use it to improve gardens and lawns, fill containers and grade the ground around buildings, though it suits potting less well than {{ref:soil-agri-028}} or compost. In the UK it must be classified under British Standard BS 3882 (2015), with thresholds for nutrients, phytotoxic elements, particle size, {{ref:soil-found-045}}, pH and contamination. The United States has no federal legal definition of it. Low-quality artificial topsoil helped rehabilitate an open-cut coal mine in Victoria, Australia.

soil-fert-149.title: Soil fertility: what lets a field feed a crop year after year
soil-fert-149.text: A fertile soil does far more than hold a plant upright. Soil fertility is the ability of a soil to sustain agricultural plant growth, giving plants a habitat and steady, high-quality yields. Such a soil supplies essential nutrients and water in adequate amounts and proportions. It is also free of toxic substances, such as Fe2+, that inhibit growth. Several properties add up to fertility. A fertile soil is deep enough for roots and stored water, drains and breathes well inside, and has an organic-rich topsoil. Its nutrients are in plant-available forms, and its microorganisms support plant growth. A soil pH between 5.5 and 7.0 suits most plants, though some prefer or tolerate more acid or alkaline conditions. Beneath all this runs constant cycling. Microbes decomposing plant and animal wastes release inorganic nutrients, while microbes competing with plants tie them up again. Negatively charged clay and humus hold nutrient cations, such as potassium and many {{ref:soil-fert-290}}, by cation exchange, which strongly influences fertility. Growing crops does not by itself exhaust a soil, as long as mineral weathering replaces the nutrients carried off in harvests. Improper irrigation and acid rain can still deplete it. On farmed land, keeping fertility usually requires conserving the soil itself, because erosion and other degradation lower soil quality. History shows the cost of neglect. Colonial land practices, slavery, and the rise of intensive farming and forestry have all damaged soil fertility and quality.

soil-bio-314.title: Forests, farmland and soil carbon
soil-bio-314.text: Cutting down a forest typically lowers its {{ref:soil-env-106}}, and planting trees again may partly restore the original levels. The rate varies. Boreal reforestation gains carbon more slowly than other climates because trees grow slowly, and the previous {{ref:soil-agri-221}} and the type of disturbance control the rate. Afforested farmland gains more carbon in the soil than pasture or grassland, and mine-disturbed soils also gain a lot. Where they suit the site, deciduous trees raise it faster than conifers. Over time they also store more of it in the mineral soil than in the forest floor.

soil-chem-176.title: Electron acceptors, the last stop for every electron
soil-chem-176.text: All organisms get energy by moving electrons from a donor to an acceptor. An electron acceptor is a chemical species that takes up electrons transferred from another compound, so it is an oxidizing agent, described in {{ref:soil-chem-114}}. Its pull is measured by its redox potential. In biology, the terminal electron acceptor receives the last electron in a transport chain, such as oxygen in aerobic respiration, though organisms use many kinds. The weedkiller paraquat is a potent acceptor: it takes electrons from {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and passes them to oxygen, forming toxic reactive oxygen species.

soil-phys-148.title: How oxygen finds its way into the ground
soil-phys-148.text: Soil air is never still. Its gas molecules move constantly, colliding and bouncing in a random walk. Gas {{ref:soil-phys-240}} is the net movement of those molecules through soil pores from higher to lower concentration. It is the main way {{ref:soil-phys-146}} trades with the atmosphere, and Fick's law describes it in numbers. Oxygen diffuses in from the air above and is consumed below. Excess carbon dioxide, other gases and water vapor diffuse out. The rate depends on total porosity, how well the pores connect, water content, air turbulence and temperature. Pore size itself matters less. Compaction lowers its coefficient, the measure of how readily gas spreads, and a platy structure also blocks the flow. Water is the great obstacle. In saturated soil no open air passages remain, and it slows some 10,000 times. Short of oxygen, anaerobic bacteria, which live without free oxygen, reduce nitrate to N2, N2O and NO gases. This drains nitrogen from the soil. Daily and seasonal swings in temperature and moisture change the soil gas, and with it the pace of {{ref:soil-bio-033}}. When frozen soils thaw or dry soils are rewetted, microbes surge into activity. Sudden bursts of carbon dioxide and methane follow.

soil-form-040.title: Pedocals, the carbonate soils of an older scheme
soil-form-040.text: Marbut's classification split soils at its highest level into two groups: pedocals and {{ref:soil-class-042}}, the latter rich in aluminum and iron. Pedocals are soils of semiarid and arid regions, rich in calcium carbonate and low in {{ref:soil-found-045}}. They were once a class of the order described in {{ref:soil-class-015}}. Under a thin A horizon, calcite and other soluble minerals that water would normally remove build up in the B horizon. There they form a cemented layer, {{ref:soil-chem-036}}. The term is not used in the current US classification, but it often appears in college geology texts.

soil-class-001.title: Putting the world's soils in order
soil-class-001.text: Long before modern science, priests in Egypt were sorting soils. Inscriptions at the temple of Horus at Edfu record a soil classification used to choose temple sites, and ancient Greek scholars devised several more. Soil classification is the systematic grouping of soils by their distinguishing characteristics and by criteria that guide how they are used. Modern systems group soils by measurable traits such as texture, structure, mineral composition and the way the soil formed. Soil science, engineering and environmental management all classify soils, to judge their properties and decide on suitable {{ref:soil-agri-221}}. Soil can be treated as a material, as geotechnical engineers do when judging foundations and building material, or as a resource. The major modern systems include {{ref:soil-class-006}}, the {{ref:soil-class-016}} and engineering systems that judge stability and performance, met in {{ref:soil-class-002}}. Standard systems matter because they let soils be compared across regions and uses. Knowledge of where soils occur has also grown dramatically. The project of {{ref:soil-meth-017}} now maps soils worldwide at 1.00–0.25 km resolution, built from soil profiles and environmental data. Still, the subject keeps moving. The structure of systems, the definitions of classes and their use in the field all continue to change.

soil-chem-173.title: Manganese in soil, a nutrient steered by pH and pe
soil-chem-173.text: In {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, manganese acts as a catalyst in the oxygen-evolving complex of photosystem II. That makes it a key soil micronutrient, one whose solubility is set by redox potential and pH. Fungi in soil oxidize soluble Mn2+ and may reprecipitate it as manganese oxides. Much of the soil cycle is biological, though inorganic reactions also oxidize manganese. As pH rises, manganese speciation becomes less sensitive to pe. In acidic soils, at pH 5 with pe above 8, manganese is mostly in reducible forms. There, exchangeable and soluble manganese fall sharply as pe rises.

soil-phys-150.title: Letting the soil breathe
soil-phys-150.text: Compaction is one of the commonest reasons a soil runs short of air. Soil aeration is the exchange of gases between soil and atmosphere, along with the ways of improving it. Below ground, microbial activity and root respiration use up oxygen and build up carbon dioxide. A lack of oxygen can then hold back plant growth. Good aeration also lets water drain and roots grow. The pore network ventilates the soil, and wind, atmospheric pressure, convection and {{ref:soil-phys-240}} all drive the exchange. Soil structure strongly shapes the larger pores that control aeration, infiltration and drainage. Those pores fail in two common ways: water fills them, or compaction crushes them. Either way, nutrient uptake can fall, and bacteria short of free oxygen take it from nitrate instead. Remedies range from chemistry to animals. Liquid aeration applies solutions, commonly of ammonium lauryl sulfate, that break down dense particles and loosen compacted soil. Adding lime improves soil structure and so aeration. Digging megafauna, large burrowing animals, help too by disturbing the soil's layers.

soil-form-062.title: Cheluviation: metals ride organic carriers downward
soil-form-062.text: A gray-white leached layer above a dark brown or red one is a typical signature of cheluviation. In this process, metal ions in the upper soil bind with organic molecules called ligands, forming chelates. The chelates move downward by eluviation and are then deposited. Iron, aluminum, manganese, calcium, magnesium and {{ref:soil-fert-290}} can all be chelated, mostly by ligands from {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Chelates with the organic acid described in {{ref:soil-chem-060}} leach and deposit strongly. Iron and aluminum move easily at low pH and under reducing conditions, but precipitate as pH rises to around 7–8 or under oxidizing conditions. Clay adsorbs chelates and weakens their leaching, while coarse-textured or water-saturated soils enhance it.

soil-chem-076.title: The chemistry hidden in a handful of soil
soil-chem-076.text: Nine-tenths of a soil's weight is rock-born. Minerals, derived from the parent rock or regolith, make up about 90% of the total weight of soil. Soil chemistry is the study of the chemical characteristics of soil, and those characteristics depend on three things: mineral composition, {{ref:soil-found-045}} and environmental factors. Plants take part too. They trade the elements they feed on with microorganisms, and they absorb them. That creates concentration gradients of cations and anions, the positively and negatively charged ions. Each of these elements follows its own cycle through rock, air, water and life. Nitrogen passes from a gas into nitrate and nitrite, while phosphorus moves in mineral form held in rock. The field has a founder. In the early 1870s J. Thomas Way, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society of England, ran many experiments on how soils exchange ions. He is considered the father of soil chemistry. Until the late 1960s the questions stayed close to the farm: the reactions behind soil formation and plant growth. On farms today the chemistry still serves plant feeding, the fertility of soil and the ingredients farmers spread to feed crops. Concern over pollution then shifted the field toward the environment, the turn traced in {{ref:soil-chem-077}}.

soil-chem-106.title: Sesquioxide clays, the last residue of deep weathering
soil-chem-106.text: A sesquioxide clay takes hundreds of thousands of years of leaching to form. These old, highly leached clays are oxides and hydroxides of iron, aluminium and titanium. They remain after heavy rainfall removes most of the silica from alumino-silica clays. They include hematite, iron hydroxide, gibbsite and the manganese mineral birnessite, as in the lateritic weathering profiles of tropical soils. The name comes from the Latin sesqui, 'one and one-half', for three parts oxygen to two of metal. Not all of them fit that ratio. They are not sticky and do not swell. Soils rich in them, such as lateritic soils, behave much like sand and pass water rapidly. Their {{ref:soil-chem-046}} is low, but because their charge varies, they can hold anions as well as cations. They hold large amounts of phosphate, a hold that humified {{ref:soil-found-045}} partly blocks. The more goethite they contain, the more phosphorus is locked away from plants. Their dominant iron oxides color these soils from yellow to red.

soil-chem-058.title: Humic substances, the dark core of soil organic matter
soil-chem-058.text: Most {{ref:soil-found-045}} is not fresh leaves or roots but something darker and older. Humic substances are dark, relatively decay-resistant organic compounds that form as biomass residues break down and change over long periods. They make up most of the organic material in soil, {{ref:soil-class-070}}, coal and sediments, and much of the organic material dissolved in lakes, rivers and sea water. Their color runs from bright yellow through brown to black, and the name comes from the Latin word for 'soil, earth'. Microbes make them from dead material such as {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, cellulose and charred wood. Yet how they form is among the least understood parts of the chemistry of this material. Maillard proposed a sugar-amine condensation theory in 1911, and Waksman, in 1932, a theory built on that woody compound. Those formed in soil over hundreds to thousands of years carry more oxygen and nitrogen than those from coal, formed over millions. Chemists split them by solubility into three fractions. They also supply 50 to 90% of a soil's {{ref:soil-chem-046}}.

soil-chem-068.title: Sorption: the many ways one substance sticks to another
soil-chem-068.text: Some {{ref:soil-found-045}} is more than a century old, and part of the reason is that it is stuck. Sorption is any physical and chemical process by which one substance becomes attached to another. It covers absorption into a substance of a different state, adsorption of ions and molecules onto the surface of another phase, and the swapping of ions. For a dilute solute, the rates of adsorption and absorption can be calculated with Fick's laws of diffusion. Much soil {{ref:soil-bio-089}} persists for over 100 years partly because it is tightly sorbed or bound to clays, out of reach of microbes and their enzymes. Sorption also steers nutrients. Molybdenum is sorbed most strongly in acid soils, so adding lime often relieves a shortage of molybdenum by loosening that hold. Aluminum sorbed onto exposed hydroxyl groups gives the edges of clay plates a slight positive charge. Those edges stick to the negative faces of other particles, and the clay flocculates. In {{ref:soil-chem-019}}, ammonium from {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, a strongly sorbing cation, trades places with weakly sorbing sodium and releases it into the water.

soil-chem-049.title: Variable charge: soil surfaces that shift with pH
soil-chem-049.text: Part of a soil's grip on nutrients turns up and down with acidity. Variable charge is surface charge on clay edges and {{ref:soil-found-045}} that changes with the pH of the soil water. It comes from hydroxyl groups, pairs of oxygen and hydrogen atoms, that give up their hydrogen ions. The broken edges of clay sheets expose many acidic hydroxyl groups. At the pH of many soils these lose their hydrogen and leave negative charges behind. Organic material in soil does the same: hydrogens on its hydroxyl groups ionize into solution, leaving an oxygen with a negative charge. Its many charged groups give it a large share of a soil's power to hold cations, positively charged ions, and that share depends heavily on pH. Raising the pH means fewer hydrogen ions in solution. More groups then lose their hydrogen, the variable charge grows, and so does the {{ref:soil-chem-046}}.

soil-chem-064.title: Does organic matter feed plants? A dispute since the 18th century
soil-chem-064.text: People once believed plants fed directly on {{ref:soil-bio-089}}. Then Liebig showed that plants grow on inorganic compounds, and {{ref:soil-found-045}} came to be valued only for the nutrients it released as it broke down. Soil scientists now at least agree that it affects fertility by helping soil hold water. Its other effects on plants have been disputed since the 18th century. Plants may absorb soluble humic material, perhaps to take up iron, but this is not settled. Studies found humic products boosted growth even at low rates.

soil-chem-063.title: Do humic substances exist, or does the lab make them?
soil-chem-063.text: Since the 18th century, soil chemists have pulled organic material out of soil with alkali. That alkaline extraction led to a theory: a process called {{ref:soil-bio-090}} creates distinct humic acid, fulvic acid and {{ref:soil-bio-105}}. Critics now ask whether these substances exist in soil at all, or are made by the extraction itself. Modern analysis of unprocessed mineral soil has not directly observed large humic molecules. That suggests extraction alters the material it is meant to reveal. Because humic and fulvic acids are defined by the separation, it is unclear whether the categories reflect the natural state of {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Some researchers argue that the method misrepresents humic substances because it uses highly alkaline extracts rather than water. Yet that theory persists, even in textbooks. Attempts to redefine humic substances have produced conflicting definitions, which hamper communication across the field. The question stays open: the old fractions may describe real soil, or they may be products of the flask.

soil-chem-047.title: Cation exchange: how soil trades nutrients with its water
soil-chem-047.text: Calcium, potassium and ammonium do not simply wash through a good soil. They cling to it, loosely, and trade places with other ions in the soil water. That trading is cation exchange: negatively charged sites on soil colloids attract positively charged ions and swap them with ions in solution. It is one case of ion exchange, a reversible swap of like-charged ions between an insoluble solid and the surrounding solution. Natural exchangers include zeolites, montmorillonite, clay and {{ref:soil-found-045}}. The hold is weak. Held cations keep a shell of water and form no direct chemical bond with the surface, so other cations displace them easily. Some cations win more often than others: at equal amounts Al3+ replaces H+, which replaces Ca2+, then Mg2+, then K+ and NH4+, then Na+. Sheer numbers can also win. A cation added in large amounts, as in potash or lime, crowds out the rest, an effect called the law of mass action. As soil water turns more acidic, hydrogen ions take over exchange sites and push weakly held cations into solution. Plants can then use them, but they can also be leached away. Roots exploit this, making organic acids that release H+ and free cations next to the root. Exchange also buffers soil pH, alters soil structure and cleans percolating water by holding both useful and harmful cations. Because held cations resist washing downward, they preserve fertility where rainfall is moderate and temperatures are low.

soil-chem-046.title: Cation-exchange capacity, the measure of a soil's nutrient store
soil-chem-046.text: A soil's store of calcium, potassium and ammonium has a ceiling, and electric charge sets it. Cation-exchange capacity, or CEC, measures how many positively charged ions a soil can hold on the surfaces of its particles. Negative charges on those surfaces bind the cations but let them swap with others in the surrounding soil water. CEC is the exchangeable positive charge per mass of soil, usually given in centimoles of charge per kilogram, cmolc/kg. Older texts use the equivalent me/100g or meq/100g. Because it counts charge, a CEC of 10 cmolc/kg could hold 10 cmol of singly charged Na+ per kilogram. It could hold only 5 cmol of doubly charged Ca2+. Most of the charge sits on clay minerals and {{ref:soil-found-045}}. So CEC is usually highest near the surface, where it is richest, and falls with depth. Soils differ enormously. Measured at pH 7, average CEC in US soils runs from 3.5 cmolc/kg in {{ref:soil-class-104}} through 18.7 in {{ref:soil-class-101}} and 35.6 in {{ref:soil-class-106}} to 128 in {{ref:soil-class-098}}. Parent material and the conditions of formation set a soil's CEC. The same factors set its pH, which has a major influence on CEC in turn. Hot, wet climates leach and decompose fast, leaving little clay or organic matter, which explains the apparent infertility of tropical soils. CEC therefore serves as a measure of fertility. It shows how well a soil keeps nutrients such as K+, NH4+ and Ca2+ within reach of plants. It also shows how much of a pollutant cation such as Pb2+ the soil can hold.

soil-chem-115.title: Reducing agents, the electron givers
soil-chem-115.text: In soil, the main giver of electrons is {{ref:soil-found-045}}. A reducing agent reduces another substance by giving it electrons, and is itself oxidized. It is also called a reductant, the role taken up in {{ref:soil-chem-177}}. Electropositive metals such as lithium, sodium, magnesium, iron, zinc and aluminium give up electrons readily, which makes them good reducing agents. Underground, donors include that same material, hydrogen, methane, reduced sulfur and iron compounds, and ammonium. Biochemists speak of a reducing equivalent: whatever transfers the equivalent of one electron, whether an electron or a hydrogen atom.

soil-chem-177.title: Electron donors: the fuel behind natural cleanup
soil-chem-177.text: {{ref:soil-found-045}}, petroleum hydrocarbons and even vinyl chloride can all hand electrons to microbes. An electron donor is a chemical species that transfers electrons to another compound, acting as a reducing agent, the role described in {{ref:soil-chem-115}}, and being oxidized itself. In respiration, donors release electrons and energy. Microbes capture that energy as the electrons pass along a transport chain to an electron acceptor. Less chlorinated solvents and reduced inorganic compounds serve as donors too. These reactions drive the natural breakdown of organic contaminants by microbes, a major part of the monitored cleanup described in {{ref:soil-env-026}}.

soil-chem-128.title: Breathing without oxygen: anaerobic respiration
soil-chem-128.text: A few millimetres of standing water are enough to smother a soil. Under that thin layer, bacteria that feed on {{ref:soil-found-045}} use up the oxygen, forcing a switch to anaerobic respiration. This is respiration that ends its electron transport chain with an inorganic acceptor other than oxygen, such as nitrate, sulfate or sulfur. These acceptors have lower reduction potentials than oxygen, so less energy is released and the process is less efficient. It differs from fermentation, which passes electrons to organic compounds. Even well-aired soil holds oxygen-free pockets, because oxygen gas diffuses slowly. The products leave their mark. Nitrate respiration is the main route returning fixed nitrogen to the air as N2. Sulfate respiration makes hydrogen sulfide, the rotten-egg smell of coastal marshes. Aerobic respiration releases carbon dioxide, while anaerobic pathways such as {{ref:soil-chem-129}} release methane. Others change the oxidation state of iron and manganese. Bacterial sulfate reduction was discovered by the scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-016}}. Because decay in waterlogged soils runs without oxygen, those soils store large amounts of organic carbon.

soil-chem-125.title: How a flooded soil runs out of oxygen
soil-chem-125.text: Flood a soil warmer than about 5 °C, and its microbes strip out the oxygen within a few days. Reduction in waterlogged soils is that shift from oxidizing to reducing conditions as oxygen runs out and anaerobic microbes take over. The fuel is {{ref:soil-found-045}}, the main source of electrons in soil. Decomposers consume oxygen as they break it down, and Eh falls. Next, nitrate and ferric oxide are reduced. Iron tells the story. At high redox potential it is deposited as ferric hematite, the oxidized form. Under low redox conditions ferrous iron builds up, and decay slows. Prolonged saturation can dissolve ferric iron minerals that hold phosphorus, releasing it to leaching. Hydrology rules the process. Flooding turns soil from oxic to anoxic, and draining and drying restore its starting Eh. Even soil that is not saturated can hold small anoxic hotspots inside its pores.

soil-bio-011.title: Soil microbiology and the 33,000 species on a beet root
soil-bio-011.text: In 2011, researchers detected more than 33,000 bacterial and archaeal species on the roots of sugar beet. Soil microbiology studies such microorganisms: what they do and how they affect soil properties. Its subjects are grouped as bacteria, including cyanobacteria and actinomycetes, archaea, fungi, algae, slime molds and {{ref:soil-bio-274}}. Their history is long. The first cyanobacteria arose two to four billion years ago. They fixed carbon and nitrogen, releasing oxygen into the air and nitrogen into the soil. How diverse a soil's microbes are depends on its pH, texture, {{ref:soil-found-045}} content, plant community and contaminants such as heavy metals. That diversity pays off. Microbes make soil nutrients more available to plants, produce growth hormones, stimulate plant immunity and trigger or dampen plant stress responses. A more diverse soil microbiome, the whole community of soil microbes, generally brings fewer plant diseases and higher crop yields. The microbes also signal to one another through soluble metabolites, volatile organic compounds and extracellular sugar polymers. They trade metabolites that support each other's growth. Farmers can encourage them: sowing {{ref:soil-agri-066}} raises microbial activity, improving nitrogen availability, crop nitrogen uptake and yields.

soil-bio-005.title: Why ecologists treat soil as an ecosystem
soil-bio-005.text: Soil organisms live under constant threat of drying out. Soil ecology studies how they interact with one another and with their environment. It is especially concerned with nutrient cycling, the formation of soil aggregates and {{ref:soil-bio-008}}. Because soil is so complex and internally connected, soil ecologists regard it as an ecosystem in its own right. It is an uneven mix of minerals and {{ref:soil-found-045}}, and its variations in structure, nutrients, moisture, temperature and pH support different organisms. Moisture is a major limit, and microbial communities shift through cycles of drying and rewetting. Temperature swings less with depth and governs microbial and enzyme activity, the release of nutrients and the pace of decay. Most soil organisms need oxygen. Microbes grow in air-filled micropores, while larger animals need macropores or water films to move. Patchy soils across a landscape, and changes between horizons, make communities patchy and layered with depth. Yet soil organisms remain underrepresented in studies and models, partly from an assumption that much below-ground diversity is ecologically redundant.

soil-bio-078.title: Burning a sample to measure its organic carbon
soil-bio-078.text: To count the organic carbon in a sample, a lab burns it. Total organic carbon is that analytical measure: the concentration of organic carbon present. The carbon is oxidized to carbon dioxide, for example by combustion at 1000 to 1200 °C or on a catalyst at 680 to 950 °C. Most modern analyzers read the gas by non-dispersive infrared. They measure only total carbon, which adds inorganic carbon, such as that in carbonate minerals, to the organic part. So the inorganic share is subtracted, or driven off first with acid. {{ref:soil-found-045}} content can be calculated from the result, and in the UK, guideline values for pollutants such as phenol and toluene depend on it. The measure also serves as a general indicator of water quality and as the first chemical test on potential petroleum source rock.

soil-bio-040.title: The earthworm, which Darwin ranked among history's great movers
soil-bio-040.text: In 1881 Charles Darwin wrote that few other animals had played so important a part in the history of the world. He meant the earthworm, a soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida. The name covers the largest members of the Oligochaeta. Earthworms live mostly in moist, compost-rich soil. They eat the remains of dead plants and animals, along with {{ref:soil-bio-274}}, {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, bacteria, fungi and algae, and rank among nature's most important eaters of dead matter.
