Adults range from 10 mm to 3 m long, though the typical common earthworm grows to about 360 mm. A worm moves by waves of muscle contraction, anchored by bristles called setae. It has no special respiratory organs and breathes through its moist skin. Populations depend on soil temperature, moisture, pH, salts, aeration and texture. Most favor neutral to slightly acidic soils, and their activity can shift pH to suit them. As they feed and burrow they aerate and mix the soil, help release nutrients for plants to take up, and bind {{ref:soil-found-045}} to soil minerals. That makes them indicators of soil health. Healthy soil holds more of them, and their gut microbes reveal its condition. They are also vulnerable. {{ref:soil-fert-007}} create acidity fatal to worms, and pesticides kill them. At least three species are listed as extinct and many more as endangered.

soil-bio-025.title: The soil food web, a digestive system for the land
soil-bio-025.text: All {{ref:soil-found-045}} passes through a living gut of sorts. The soil food web is the community of organisms living all or part of their lives in soil. It is seen as a network of feeding links that passes energy among them. A food chain follows one linear energy pathway; a food web shows all the potential pathways. Plants are the producers. Using sunlight, they make plant material from carbon dioxide and minerals, and their roots exude acids, sugars and enzymes that feed the web underground. Its members range from bacteria, algae, fungi and single-celled animals to {{ref:soil-bio-193}} and {{ref:soil-bio-209}}, and on to earthworms, insects and small vertebrates. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break dead plant and animal material into simple nutrients. In this way the web processes dead material much as a digestive system processes food. The work reaches beyond the soil. The web keeps manure, plant residues and pesticides out of water, holds nitrogen back from groundwater, fixes nitrogen and helps water soak in. Its members prey on crop pests and feed animals above ground. Once thought simple, soil food webs turned out to have common omnivory and long, complex chains. Those chains still resist drying, freezing and fumigation. Some influence escapes the diagram, though. Litter transformers, mutualists and {{ref:soil-bio-004}} strongly affect their communities in ways food webs do not capture.

soil-bio-033.title: Soil respiration: the ground breathes out carbon
soil-bio-033.text: Each year the world's soils release an estimated 77 Pg of carbon, more than human sources such as fossil fuel burning. That flow is soil respiration: the carbon dioxide produced by respiring roots, the microbes around them and soil animals below ground. It is a key ecosystem process. Carbon fixed by {{ref:soil-hist-147}} returns to the air as CO2, respired either by roots or by the heterotrophs that consume plant material. Rates vary enormously with temperature, moisture, nutrient content and oxygen. Inside soil aggregates, oxygen gradients create anoxic microsites, tiny oxygen-free pockets where anaerobic metabolism dominates. Decaying litter is a major part of the total. It releases CO2 while locking up or freeing nutrients, so respiration rates track microbial turnover and the release of mineral nitrogen. Turning the soil with {{ref:soil-agri-095}} usually increases soil respiration, depleting {{ref:soil-found-045}}. The stakes are global. Soils hold up to 3150 Pg of carbon, more than four times the atmosphere, so a small change in soil respiration can upset the balance of atmospheric CO2. Between 1989 and 2008 soil respiration rose by about 0.1% per year. Respiration also forms a positive feedback with climate: warming raises it, and so raises CO2. A 2 °C rise is estimated to add 10 Pg of carbon a year from soils.

soil-bio-039.title: Soil enzymes, the chemical tools of decay
soil-bio-039.text: Microbes face a problem of scale: much of their food comes as large molecules left by dead plants and animals. Soil enzymes solve it. Released mainly by microbes, they break down {{ref:soil-found-045}} and free nutrients for plants. Fungi, bacteria and archaea excrete them, and plant roots produce some. They speed the breakdown of compounds such as cellulose, starch and {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, which makes them prominent agents in the cycling of carbon and nitrogen. Some work inside cells, some stay attached to cells, and some float free. Enzymes bound to clay and humic particles are protected from rapid breakdown but are less active, a trade-off between protection and activity. Their spread is highly patchy, varying at the millimeter scale with nutrients, microbes and roots, and from single trees to whole catchments. Farming steers them. Some fertilizers include {{ref:soil-fert-085}}, which hold back the enzyme that breaks down that compound so nutrients are released over a longer period. Enzyme activity was higher with manure than with inorganic fertilizer, though other studies found a mix of mineral and organic inputs better still. Enzymes both stabilize and degrade soil structure, and they play a decisive role in keeping soil healthy.

soil-bio-004.title: Ecosystem engineers, the builders of soil habitat
soil-bio-004.text: Some species matter less for who eats them than for what they build. Ecosystem engineers are species that create, significantly modify, maintain or destroy a habitat. In soil they are chiefly burrowing animals such as earthworms, ants and termites, along with fungi. Engineers are defined by how they modify resources for other organisms, not by being eaten, which sets them apart from keystone species. Allogenic engineers change materials mechanically, as burrowers do. Autogenic engineers create habitat with their own bodies, as Sphagnum moss builds {{ref:soil-water-136}}. Earthworms, ants and termites mix the soil as they burrow. They strongly affect soil formation and the fate of {{ref:soil-found-045}} while building crumbly, granular structure. Ant and termite nests enrich soil in carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus and mix particles from different depths. Moles, gophers and prairie dogs turn soil, spread fungi that partner with roots, and open corridors used by arthropods, birds, small mammals and reptiles. Fungi are engineers too. By linking distant patches and moving nutrients between them, even shifting carbon between trees, they control nutrient cycles. Where earthworms do little, potworms take on the role, digging galleries in which they leave their feces. Earthworms are particularly sensitive to many contaminants, and losing such engineers dramatically changes the organic layers at the soil surface. Not everyone likes the term. Some ecologists call it a buzzword, arguing that it implies intent or that every species would qualify.

soil-bio-047.title: Bioturbation: how burrowers stir the earth
soil-bio-047.text: In the 1800s Darwin watched a field slowly swallow a layer of chalk. Spread on the surface, the chalk lay 18 centimeters deep after 30 years, a burial rate of 6 millimeters per year that he credited to earthworms. That began the formal study of bioturbation: the reworking of soils and sediments by animals or plants, through burrowing and the swallowing and excreting of grains. Walruses, salmon and pocket gophers are conspicuous bioturbators, but small invertebrates such as earthworms, polychaete worms, shrimps and midge larvae dominate. Bioturbation differs from bioirrigation, the mixing of water and dissolved substances in sediments, which is one of its effects. Burrowers carry oxygen into oxygen-poor layers, changing how microbes live and speeding the breakdown of {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Their burrows shelter other species. The process profoundly affects the environment and is thought to be a primary driver of biodiversity. Nathaniel Shaler added ants and trees to the story in 1891. Rudolf Richter coined the term in 1952, and it has been widely used in soil science and the study of landforms since the 1980s. The process itself is far older. Since it began around 539 million years ago it has changed ocean chemistry, and it is thought to have been a co-factor of the Cambrian Explosion. Pollution can run it backward. When pollution harms earthworms, termites and ants, bioturbation falls and the {{ref:soil-bio-095}} shifts toward mor.

soil-bio-048.title: Gophers, worms and fallen trees: how soil gets stirred
soil-bio-048.text: Pocket gophers may produce soil on a scale equal to non-living processes. Bioturbation in soils is the mixing and moving of soil by burrowing animals and plant roots. It matters for soil production, burial, {{ref:soil-found-045}} content and the movement of soil downslope. Plants and animals disturb the upper soil and bring weathered rock, saprolite, up from depth to the surface. Gopher mounds carry little-weathered rock up, speeding soil formation, and are easily eroded downslope. The mounds also bury plants, which decay into nutrient hotspots. Burrows, even when backfilled, lower soil density. Burrows of earthworms and small mammals carry air and water. They change porosity, nutrient content and how particle sizes are spread with depth. Trees play their part. Roots add organic material and leave voids when they rot, and uprooted trees throw up mounds and can turn sections of soil upside down. Burrowers that eat dead matter build the organic-rich topsoil called the soil biomantle, and so help form soil horizons.

soil-bio-009.title: What acid, salt and the plow do to soil life
soil-bio-009.text: In Dutch soils below pH 5, biodiversity fell as pH fell, in grasslands and heathlands alike. Threats to soil biodiversity are soil changes that reduce the variety of soil life, such as acidification, salinization, sodicity, structure decline and erosion. Many are driven by how soil is managed. Acidification cuts the numbers of most large soil animals, earthworms included. It harms the survival of the bacteria covered in {{ref:soil-bio-239}} and may slow decay and the capture of nitrogen from the air. Salt works differently. At low salinity microbes are active and soil respiration is high; as salinity rises, microbes have less available water and respire less. Prolonged high sodium leaves soil cement-like, holding and passing less water and breaking down {{ref:soil-found-045}} more slowly. Erosion strips topsoil, organic material and nutrients and breaks down structure, making it a major threat. Constant {{ref:soil-agri-095}} redistributes it, degrading structure and altering populations of earthworms and other organisms. Even a common fertilizer can harm. Chloride from potassium chloride raises salinity and is biocidal, harming the growth, survival and reproduction of soil organisms, including the bacteria that make nitrate.

soil-bio-023.title: Macrofauna, the soil animals big enough to see
soil-bio-023.text: Earthworms, termites, ants, millipedes, woodlice, beetles, slugs and snails all belong to the soil macrofauna: soil and litter invertebrates between 2 mm and 2 cm long. Earthworms, termites, ants, some millipedes and some insect larvae make pore spaces and so change soil structure. Diets differ widely. Millipedes, woodlice and some earthworms eat leaf litter. Lower termites eat wood, while endogeic earthworms and higher termites eat dark, decayed {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Centipedes and spiders hunt prey. Shredding plant remains speeds decay, and so does waking dormant bacteria in the soil the animals swallow. Researchers call this the 'Sleeping Beauty' paradigm, with the earthworm as 'Prince Charming'. Animals that eat dead matter need enzymes from gut microbes to digest wood or similar organic material. In lower termites, partner flagellates help digest the tough fibers of wood. Food ground in earthworm gizzards or chewed by termites leaves pasty feces that harden into stable earthworm casts and termite mounds. Macrofauna are abundant in fertile soils and typical of the mull type of {{ref:soil-bio-095}}, with many feeding niches and more complex food webs. They need much calcium and nitrogen, so they depend on plants with fast-decaying litter. By speeding nutrient cycling, they favor such plants in return: a positive feedback between life above and below ground.

soil-bio-015.title: The microbial loop: how predators free nutrients for roots
soil-bio-015.text: Farooq Azam, Tom Fenchel and others coined the term microbial loop in 1983 for the role of bacteria in marine carbon and nutrient cycles. It names the pathway by which bacteria take up dissolved organic carbon and pass it back up the food web. 'Microbial food web' is now often used instead. In soil, the loop concerns carbon and the nutrients freed when protozoa and {{ref:soil-bio-193}} eat bacteria fed by roots. It runs like this. Roots pushing into new soil prime resting bacteria, which naked amoebae then eat. That frees mineral nitrogen for root hairs to absorb. Predation by amoebae and free-living roundworms raises the rate at which nutrients are released, which in turn stimulates root growth. This loop is Clarholm's hypothesis, and it is hard to verify by experiment. Bacteria-eating protozoa release the nutrients locked in microbial bodies in a form plants can use. A related idea, the model in {{ref:soil-bio-266}}, has plants add carbon through {{ref:soil-bio-142}} and litter. Microbes then either respire it to the atmosphere or store it in a stable pool as dead microbial matter, called necromass. They transform plant carbon outside the cell with enzymes and inside it as their populations grow and die. The balance between pathways that release CO2 and those that build carbon sets how much carbon the soil keeps. Fresh plant carbon can also prime microbes to break down carbon already stored in {{ref:soil-found-045}} faster than models expect. Much remains unknown. Most of the soil microbiome has never been cultivated, which leaves its part in carbon cycling uncertain and hampers climate models of carbon flux.

soil-bio-276.title: Humus: the dark, stable core of soil organic matter
soil-bio-276.text: Humus is light for its bulk. Its bulk density is just 0.05 to 0.25 g per cubic centimetre, and its cation exchange capacity tops 200 cmol(+) per kilogram. It is the stable, dark, amorphous fraction of {{ref:soil-found-045}} left after most added residues have decomposed, bound to clays and oxides that shield it from microbes. It has high porosity and water holding capacity. Its approximate composition is 50% carbon, 35% oxygen, 8% hydrogen, 5% nitrogen and 2% sulfur. It commonly supplies 20 to 30% or more of a soil's cation exchange capacity, buffers pH and binds peds into aggregates. Arable soils average 2 to 3% humus, from under 1% to over 12%. Keeping it takes work. Cultivated soils lose humus by decomposition at 1 to 2% per year. Holding the normal level needs 1000 to 5000 kg per hectare of organic material a year, since added material does not permanently raise it. Rotations with grasses and legumes, {{ref:soil-agri-099}} and residue management help sustain it.

soil-bio-275.title: From residue to humus: how microbes recycle organic matter
soil-bio-275.text: Soil with 1% organic matter holds up to 45 million kilocalories per acre-furrow-slice, equivalent to about 6 tons of coal. Microbes oxidise that energy store partly to carbon dioxide, water and energy, leaving humus, new microbial cells and inorganic plant nutrients. Fresh residues decompose rapidly at first, releasing carbon dioxide, water, energy and small amounts of inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur. The microbes' most important function is recycling organic carbon to CO2, which keeps {{ref:soil-hist-147}} going. Their oxidation also turns nutrients from unavailable organic forms into plant-available inorganic ones, so organic matter acts as a slow-release fertilizer that buffers nutrient supply. The process is wasteful. Microbes use only a small share of the energy for new cells, and making one pound of {{ref:soil-found-045}} may destroy 10 to 20 pounds of residues. Fresh residues also accelerate decomposition of humified material already in the soil. The reward is structure. Added organic matter improves tilth, raises cation exchange and water holding capacity and aeration, and reduces erosion.

soil-class-006.title: USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series
soil-class-006.text: The United States sorts its soils into 12 orders, 47 suborders, about 185 great groups, about 1,000 subgroups, about 4,500 families and more than 14,000 series. USDA soil taxonomy is the classification of the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the {{ref:soil-hist-051}}. It sorts soils by their properties into six levels, from most general to most specific: order, suborder, great group, subgroup, family and series. The lab manual describes it as a quantitative hierarchy running from 12 broad orders to more than 23,000 series, and says it helps carry management research between similar soils worldwide. Sources differ on the series count: the more than 14,000 above is the United States figure. It uses properties that can be measured: depth, moisture, temperature, texture, structure, cation exchange capacity, base saturation, clay mineralogy, organic matter and salt content. It is a hierarchical hybrid of natural and objective criteria, designed to guide {{ref:soil-agri-221}} and {{ref:soil-agri-063}}, and it supplies the core criteria for U.S. soil map units. Order names end in -sol, and the criteria for orders reflect major differences in how soils formed. It builds on {{ref:soil-class-001}}, {{ref:soil-class-005}}, {{ref:soil-found-001}} and {{ref:soil-form-017}}. Guy Donald Smith, director of USDA soil survey investigations, originally developed it as a substantial revision of the strictly natural 1938 system. Work began by 1945. A series of approximations followed, the 7th in 1960, and the taxonomy appeared in 1975 with 10 orders and in 1999, revised, with 12.

soil-class-003.title: Natural classes and technical classes
soil-class-003.text: A soil can be classified for what it is, or for what it is good for. Natural systems group soils by their intrinsic properties, behavior or genesis. Technical systems group them by fitness for a particular use. Experience shows that natural classes can be interpreted for many different uses. Some natural systems, such as the French {{ref:soil-class-035}}, rest on presumed soil genesis. USDA soil taxonomy and the WRB use morphology and laboratory tests as the criteria for their hierarchical classes. Each system's approach reflects its own ideas of how soils form and of which features matter for {{ref:soil-agri-221}}. In U.S. soil mapping the two kinds meet. Map units classed by soil taxonomy are also sorted into technical classes such as Land Capability Classes, {{ref:soil-water-119}} and {{ref:soil-agri-088}}. A third route is numerical classification, or ordination. It groups soil individuals by multivariate statistics such as cluster analysis, producing natural groups without any inference about genesis.

soil-class-037.title: Soil series: named for a town, mapped across states
soil-class-037.text: Haugan, Montana, gave its name to a soil. A soil series is named after a town or landmark near where it was first recognized, yet a series such as Hagerstown can range across several states. The series is the lowest level of USDA soil taxonomy. It groups pedons with similar pedogenesis, soil chemistry and physical properties. Their horizons match in color, texture, structure, pH, consistency, composition and arrangement in the profile, so the soils perform alike for {{ref:soil-agri-221}}. The concept dates from 1903. Series were then meant as soils alike in origin, from the same kind of rock or sediment, but differing in texture. More than 14,000 series are recognized in the United States, the most homogeneous classes in the taxonomy; another source counts even more. A series can mean two things. As a taxonomic unit it is the conceptual core of a class. As a mapping unit it outlines similar soils on the land, and the two need not fully coincide. Map units carry the name of their dominant series. In Greenbrier County, West Virginia, unit LhE is 80% Lily series, and the rest is Dekalb, Berks and less stony soils.

soil-class-073.title: Peat archives, a diary kept in layers
soil-class-073.text: Peat keeps a diary. Because it builds up over thousands of years, its layers preserve pollen, spores, plants, animals and archaeological remains, letting scientists reconstruct past vegetation, climate and {{ref:soil-agri-221}}. Harry Godwin, a scientist of peat bogs, coined the phrase peat archives in 1981. Researchers compare peat records with modern bogs to gauge how people have changed the movement of mercury. They date the layers by methods such as the vertical spread of lead-210. Acidic, tanning water and an antibiotic called sphagnan preserve bog bodies almost perfectly, such as Denmark's Tollund Man, who lived in the 4th century BC.

soil-fert-151.title: Soil depletion: spending the soil's nutrient bank
soil-fert-151.text: Topsoil takes hundreds to thousands of years to form, and it can be spent far faster. Soil depletion is the decline of a soil's fertility when what makes it fertile is removed and not replaced. The conditions that support fertility are not maintained either. It leads to poor harvests and is becoming a global problem. On farms it stems from overly intensive cultivation and careless handling of the land. Over-tillage, salinization and overuse of nutrient inputs all contribute, the last of these mining the soil's nutrient bank. Rapid changes in {{ref:soil-agri-221}} can also severely challenge soil fertility. As of 2008, depletion was among the most widespread problems in tropical zones, where soils are low in nutrients. In the Middle East, drought, erosion and lack of irrigation hamper farming, and productivity has fallen most steeply in hilly and dryland areas. Across much of Africa fertile soil is being depleted, notably in the Sahel under high population pressure. Farmers there use artificial and natural fertilizers to restore nutrients. The stakes can be enormous. Topsoil depletion, the erosion or exhaustion of organic topsoil, has been blamed for the collapse of many past civilizations.

soil-fert-014.title: The hidden bill for feeding the world's crops
soil-fert-014.text: Fertilizer washing off farmland helps create dead zones in the ocean. That is one of the direct costs of fertilizers, whose production and use harm water, soil, air and ecosystems. It also contaminates waterways, the soil microbiome degrades and toxic compounds accumulate. Indirect costs reach further: nitrogen-crop-pest cascades, fracking for the gas the Haber process needs, and the biodiversity and soil loss tied to industrial agriculture. The climate pays too. Most synthetic fertilizer depends on fossil fuel, with methane supplying the hydrogen for ammonia. The IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land names fertilizer production and its associated {{ref:soil-agri-221}} among the drivers of global warming. Organic sources are not blameless, since too much pig slurry can contaminate aquifers and overfeed the waters they supply. Solar energy, waste treatment and electrolysis are proposed alternatives for production. On the farm, plowing less and planting the streamside borders of {{ref:soil-agri-158}} can lessen the damage. Policy favors sustainable or regenerative farming, with less synthetic fertilizer, better care of the soil and more of the biological fertilizers in {{ref:soil-fert-010}}.

soil-fert-025.title: What can go wrong with animal manure
soil-fert-025.text: Manure feeds the soil, but it can carry more than nutrients. Any manure may hold pathogens or food-spoilage organisms, spread by flies, rodents and other vectors, that threaten food safety. Under intensive {{ref:soil-agri-221}} it is spread less precisely than mineral fertilizer, so crops use its nitrogen poorly, and it can give off nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas. In 2007 a University of Minnesota study found corn, lettuce and potatoes taking up antibiotics from soils spread with drug-laden manure. Organic standards therefore require non-organic manure to be rotted or composted first. That breaks down drug residues and kills pathogenic bacteria.

soil-water-080.title: How clearing and building rewire the local water cycle
soil-water-080.text: Change the land cover and the water moves differently. {{ref:soil-agri-221}} and the water cycle names the local and regional changes to the water cycle that follow changes in how land is used and in land cover. Urbanization, farm expansion and deforestation can increase {{ref:soil-phys-082}} and impervious cover. Both lower the soil's infiltration capacity and raise surface runoff. Locally, clearing forest reduces soil moisture, evaporation, rainfall and snowfall. City pipes cut both ways. Stormwater drains lower runoff rates and raise groundwater recharge, while leaking sewers add recharge but can contaminate groundwater.

soil-water-088.title: The curve number, one figure for a storm's runoff
soil-water-088.text: A single number between 30 and 100 can estimate how much of a storm will run off the land. That number is the runoff curve number, CN, an empirical value used in hydrology to predict direct runoff or infiltration from rainfall excess. The US Department of Agriculture developed it, through the agency now called the {{ref:soil-hist-050}}, from runoff measured on small catchments and hillslope plots. A curve number depends on the area's {{ref:soil-water-255}}, {{ref:soil-agri-221}}, treatment and hydrologic condition. Lower numbers mean more permeable soil and low runoff potential; higher numbers mean more runoff. No runoff starts until the initial abstraction, such as infiltration and interception, is met. That threshold was long taken as 0.2 S, but 0.05 S may suit urban watersheds better. Curve numbers are adjusted for antecedent moisture: dry (AMC I), average (AMC II) and moist (AMC III). The method works storm by storm and should not be applied to a single annual rainfall total. Even so, it is widely used as an efficient way to estimate approximate direct runoff.

soil-water-102.title: Riparian buffers, green strips that guard a stream
soil-water-102.text: A nine-year University of Georgia study found that streamside buffers removed at least 60% of the nitrogen and at least 65% of the phosphorus from fertilizer in runoff. A riparian buffer is a vegetated strip beside a stream, usually forested, that shades it and partly shields it from neighboring {{ref:soil-agri-221}}. It intercepts sediment, nutrients, pesticides and other materials in surface runoff, and reduces pollutants in shallow subsurface flow. It also stabilizes the stream bank, so eroding banks take less farmland out of production and less silt reaches lakes and reservoirs downstream. A typical buffer is 15 meters (50 feet) wide on each side, in three zones. Native grasses first slow the runoff, shrubs come next, and fast-growing trees shade the water and hold the bank.

soil-water-042.title: The P factor, credit for conservation practices
soil-water-042.text: Stone walls and hedgerows held soil in place long before anyone wrote an equation for erosion. The support practice factor is the P factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation, a soil loss ratio expressing how much conservation practices reduce erosion. It is hard to determine because regional maps of conservation practices are usually lacking, so it is often estimated from {{ref:soil-agri-221}} and slope. Field boundaries such as stone walls, hedgerows, earth banks and {{ref:soil-agri-081}} effectively prevented or reduced erosion in pre-industrial farming. A European P-factor model was built from a survey that recorded stone walls and grass margins, and landscape archaeology mapping can fill gaps in the data.

soil-water-291.title: RUSLE, the soil loss equation revised
soil-water-291.text: An equation first built for farm fields is still among North America's busiest erosion tools. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation, or RUSLE, is an updated form of {{ref:soil-water-041}}. With the WEPP model, it is one of the two most widely used erosion models on the continent. Various techniques now compute its five factors. The support practice factor, P, is often estimated from {{ref:soil-agri-221}} and slope gradient, and a lower value means better erosion control. Much research on eroding mined land focuses on fitting or improving its parameters.

soil-water-061.title: Mapping where the next landslide will strike
soil-water-061.text: Landslide hazard mapping rests on one assumption: future slides will happen under the same conditions as past ones. Analysts study the factors behind earlier landslides, usually grouped as {{ref:soil-water-295}}, geology, {{ref:soil-agri-221}} and land cover, and hydrogeology. Mapping software, the subject of {{ref:soil-agri-165}}, handles the many layered factors. Aerial photos and satellite images taken before and after events record where slides happened and what set them off. A good hazard map shows past events and clearly marks probable future sites, so planners can reduce losses.

soil-agri-140.title: Agroforestry: farming with the forest as a model
soil-agri-140.text: The forester John Bene coined the word agroforestry in 1973, but the practices it names are millennia old. Agroforestry is a {{ref:soil-agri-221}} system that integrates trees with crops or pasture. It is managed to optimize the interactions among plants and animals, with the forest as its model, which makes it applied agroecology. Groundcover protects depleted soil from erosion, and trees slow runoff and evaporation so more water soaks in. Nitrogen-fixing plants such as legumes can restore soil nitrogen fertility. Carbon can build up in both soil and woody biomass. The USDA lists five temperate practices: alley cropping, forest farming, riparian forest buffers, silvopasture and {{ref:soil-agri-061}}. In Honduras, the Quesungual system replaced slash-and-burn hillside farming, whose exposed soil washed away. It keeps nitrogen-fixing trees that cut erosion and hold moisture. In 2025, 91 countries and areas reported 55.4 million hectares under agroforestry, most of it in Asia.

soil-chem-137.title: Halotolerance: living with more salt than needed
soil-chem-137.text: Salt pulls water out of living cells. Halotolerance is the ability of an organism to live in salt concentrations above those it needs for growth. Halotolerant bacteria, archaea and fungi live in saline waters and soils; unlike halophiles, they do not need high salinity. High salt upsets ionic balance, impairing respiration and {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and slowing growth or killing sensitive plants. Because salinity brings both osmotic and ionic stress, tolerant organisms retain water and sequester salt. Halotolerant bacteria can even remediate saline soil, lowering its sodium content and sodium adsorption ratio and degrading toxic compounds.

soil-bio-077.title: Sorting bacteria by how they eat and breathe
soil-bio-077.text: Bacteria can be sorted by three questions: where their energy comes from, which electron donors they use and where they get their carbon. Electrons are the currency of {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. Phototrophs get their energy from light by {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, while the organisms of {{ref:soil-bio-205}} get it by oxidizing chemical compounds. Bacteria that take electrons from inorganic compounds such as hydrogen, carbon monoxide or ammonia are covered in {{ref:soil-bio-056}}; those that use organic compounds are the subject of {{ref:soil-bio-206}}. Heterotrophs take their carbon from organic compounds, while autotrophs such as cyanobacteria and some purple bacteria fix carbon dioxide. Aerobes use oxygen as the final electron acceptor, and anaerobes use nitrate, sulfate or carbon dioxide. Facultative anaerobes switch between fermentation and different acceptors as conditions change.

soil-bio-036.title: Putting a lid on the soil to measure its breath
soil-bio-036.text: To measure how fast soil breathes, researchers put a lid on it. A closed chamber is sealed over the soil, and the flux comes from how fast CO2 builds up over a few minutes, using F=bV/A. Longer runs underestimate it, because some CO2 is stored in the soil instead. Open systems pump fresh air through the chamber and read the flux at equilibrium. Basal respiration is measured with nothing added; substrate-induced respiration adds nutrients and sugars. Stable carbon isotopes reveal where the CO2 comes from. Swapping C3 and C4 crops, plants with two different kinds of {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, or spraying C4 cane sugar, tells old carbon from new and microbial respiration from root respiration.

soil-bio-034.title: Roots, microbes and animals: who breathes out soil CO2
soil-bio-034.text: Roughly half the CO2 rising from soil comes from roots. Root respiration accounts for approximately half of {{ref:soil-bio-033}}, though values range from 10 to 90% with plant type and conditions. The rest comes from the organisms around them. Up to 20% of the carbon a plant captures in {{ref:soil-hist-147}} leaks into the soil from roots, and bacteria decompose most of it. Fungi partnered with roots also respire sugars the plant gives them. Most of the CO2 comes from the TCA cycle of cellular respiration. Fermentation, which works without oxygen, adds more in the oxygen-poor soil right around roots. Soil animals contribute by grazing bacteria and fungi and by fragmenting litter, which exposes more surface to microbes.

soil-bio-207.title: Light or chemicals, rock or food: how life gets fed
soil-bio-207.text: Every living thing must answer three questions: where do its energy, its electrons and its carbon come from? The answers sort life into primary nutritional groups. Energy comes from light, for phototrophs, or from chemical compounds, for {{ref:soil-bio-205}}. Electrons come from organic donors, as in {{ref:soil-bio-206}}, or from inorganic ones, for lithotrophs. Carbon comes from organic compounds, for heterotrophs, or from carbon dioxide, for autotrophs. A name combines one term from each pair. A chemoorganoheterotroph, for example, takes its carbon from organic substrates and its energy from breaking down an organic compound. The pairs often travel together. Organisms that draw electrons from organic matter are often heterotrophs too, and lithotrophs are often autotrophs that use carbon dioxide. Plants count as lithotrophs because water is the electron donor of their {{ref:soil-hist-147}}. Cyanobacteria, algae and land plants are therefore photolithoautotrophs. Decomposers are chemoorganoheterotrophs, taking carbon and electrons from dead organic matter. All animals, fungi and protozoa, and some bacteria, are chemoheterotrophs. The labels are not always fixed: plants and some bacteria can switch between phototrophy and chemotrophy depending on the light. One distinction is easy to confuse. Aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration and fermentation describe the electron acceptor used, the substance that finally takes the electrons, and do not define a nutritional group.

soil-bio-280.title: Roots as soil engineers
soil-bio-280.text: Corn sends about 20 percent of its {{ref:soil-hist-147}} sugars to its roots early to mid-season. Roots influence soil as much as soil influences them, shaping aggregates and feeding soil organisms. Root pressure brings particles closer, small roots bind them, and root hairs add soil contact for water and nutrient access and help form aggregates. Roots exude compounds that feed organisms in the surrounding zone. Mucigel, a sticky layer around roots, gives close contact between microorganisms, soil minerals and the plant. Roots add organic matter that may decompose more slowly than surface residues, and in grasses the living tissue below ground can exceed that above. They do not grow well in compact, nutrient- or water-poor, high-pathogen or extreme-pH soil.

soil-hist-015.title: The Winogradsky column: a jar of sediment as an ecosystem
soil-hist-015.text: A jar of mud can teach a whole course in microbial metabolism. A Winogradsky column is a simple stratified microbial ecosystem built from sediment in a container. Columns are set up as a control and with added carbon (cellulose), sulfur (egg yolk calcium sulfate) or both, then form oxygen and sulfide gradients, the kind described in {{ref:soil-chem-121}}. Purple and green sulfur bacteria use sulfide to support {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, and green sulfur bacteria tolerate higher sulfide than purple. Winogradsky developed it, and discovered chemosynthesis, in his early efforts to understand microbes outside the medical context. It remains an important demonstration of chemoautotrophy and microbial ecology in microbiology lectures around the world, and a window into {{ref:soil-bio-011}}.

soil-bio-143.title: The rhizosphere, the crowded zone around every root
soil-bio-143.text: Each gram of soil in and around roots can hold up to 10 billion bacterial cells that grow in culture. In 1904 a German plant physiologist, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-075}}, named this crowded zone the rhizosphere. He meant soil around roots whose microbes are partly controlled by chemicals the roots release. Today it is defined as the narrow zone of soil directly influenced by root secretions and by the microorganisms living with the roots. The roots pay generously for their company. They may exude 20–40% of the carbon they fix by {{ref:soil-hist-147}} as sugars and organic acids. Microbes in the zone's pores feed on these root exudates and on sloughed-off root cells, a process described in {{ref:soil-bio-148}}. The result is a hotspot of microbial diversity. Much of the nutrient cycling plants need happens right beside roots, and so does disease suppression by microbial antibiotics. Organic acids and sugars affect how microbes shuttle phosphorus, nitrogen, potassium and water to the root, and how much iron is available. Root respiration and exudation can create pockets without oxygen next to roots. In acid soils, the pH rises close to roots. At the very center lies the rhizoplane: the root surface itself, with the soil particles closely bound to it.

soil-bio-157.title: Mycorrhiza, the ancient pact between root and fungus
soil-bio-157.text: In some ecosystems up to 80% of plant nitrogen and 90% of plant phosphorus reaches the plant through fungi. A mycorrhiza is the partnership behind those numbers. It is a symbiosis in which fungal hyphae, the fungus's fine threads, interconnect with plant roots and meet them at the level of single cells. The plant pays the fungus in sugars or lipids made by {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, perhaps 20–40% of its carbon. The fungus returns water and soil nutrients such as phosphorus, nitrogen and zinc. Some fungi colonize root tissue inside the cells, as in {{ref:soil-bio-166}}. Others grow between the cells, as in {{ref:soil-bio-173}}. The partnership occurs in 92% of plant families studied, covering 80% of species. Some families, such as Brassicaceae and Chenopodiaceae, cannot form it at all. A plant short of phosphorus is quick to recruit fungi, and nitrogen starvation also plays a part. The deal is normally mutualistic, good for both sides, but in some species or circumstances it turns parasitic. It is also ancient. Mycorrhizae emerged as early as 450–500 million years ago, and early fungal partners may have been key to plants colonizing land.

soil-bio-151.title: The root microbiome, the company a root keeps
soil-bio-151.text: Before the 1970s, most scientists thought microbes blanketed the whole root surface. In fact they cover about 10% of three-week-old root segments and about 37% of three-month-old roots. The root microbiome is the changing community of microorganisms, mainly bacteria, fungi and archaea, that lives with plant roots. The communities inside the root, in the rhizosphere and in bulk soil differ, though some species overlap. Helpful members include nitrogen-fixing bacteria, growth-promoting microbes, mycorrhizal fungi, protozoa and organisms that fight disease. Some bacteria, fungi and nematodes do harm. Root partners live on carbon-rich products of the host's {{ref:soil-hist-147}}. Mycorrhizal fungi stretch far into the bulk soil, widening the root system's reach. Archaea that make methane or oxidize ammonia are common, especially in wetlands and other soils without oxygen. Plants also pick their company: in finger millet, only about 8% of the core microbiota was consistently shared between soil and plant.

soil-bio-141.title: Root mucilage, the slime that greases every root tip
soil-bio-141.text: Plants use up to 40% of the energy they make by {{ref:soil-hist-147}} secreting one product: slime. Root mucilage is a gelatinous secretion of plant-specific long chains of sugars, that coats the protective tip described in {{ref:soil-bio-198}} as part of the root exudate. How it is secreted is still debated. Growing evidence points to root-cap cells that are continually shed and burst as roots push through soil, releasing sugar chains made in their Golgi apparatus and cell walls. Maize mucilage is rich in galactose, xylose, arabinose, rhamnose and glucose, the building blocks of pectin and other plant sugar polymers. Mucilage glues soil to the root, keeping the contact needed to regulate water uptake. It cuts friction as roots penetrate and maintains a microclimate. It can also reduce evaporation and store water, which helps plants cope with water deficit. Soil fungi feed on broken-down mucilage and in return raise the plant's uptake of water and nutrients, particularly phosphorus.

soil-bio-239.title: Rhizobium, the nitrogen fixer inside legume roots
soil-bio-239.text: In 1888 {{ref:soil-hist-016}} isolated a microbe from legume nodules and named it Bacillus radicicola; it is now placed in Rhizobium. This genus of aerobic, rod-shaped, nitrogen-fixing soil bacteria lives in root nodules, mainly of legumes. Inside, the bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia with an enzyme, {{ref:soil-fert-101}}. They pass it to the plant as glutamine or ureides and receive photosynthate, the products of {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, in return. Rhizobium can also solubilize phosphate. Not every member helps: Rhizobium rhizogenes causes hairy root disease by injecting root-inducing T-DNA into plants.

soil-bio-267.title: Q10: how much warmth speeds up life
soil-bio-267.text: Warm most living systems by 10 °C and their chemistry runs two to three times faster. That factor is Q10, the temperature coefficient: a unitless measure of how much a rate changes with a 10 °C rise. It assumes rates rise exponentially with temperature, following Q10 = (R2/R1)^(10 °C/(T2−T1)). It applies to processes such as respiration, including {{ref:soil-bio-033}}, and {{ref:soil-hist-147}}. Environmental scientists often use 0 °C or 10 °C as the reference. The idea is thought to come from van 't Hoff's work in the late 19th century.

soil-fert-179.title: Micronutrients: tiny doses that run every enzyme
soil-fert-179.text: Every process that supports plant growth runs through a protein containing a micronutrient. Plant micronutrients are essential elements needed only in very small amounts, mostly as required parts of enzyme systems. In order of importance they include chlorine, iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper and molybdenum. Manganese builds the structure of photosystem II and helps build chloroplasts. Copper aids {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and the forming of lignin, and chlorine serves osmosis and ionic balance. Nickel activates the enzyme of {{ref:soil-fert-224}}, which processes {{ref:soil-fert-021}}; without nickel, this nitrogen compound builds up to toxic levels and causes necrotic lesions. Molybdenum is part of nitrate reductase and of {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, the enzyme bacteria use to fix nitrogen. Soil minerals generally supply enough, but heavy phosphate use can cause zinc and iron deficiency by forming insoluble phosphates. Too little uptake causes deficiencies, such as a yellowing of leaves ({{ref:soil-fert-228}}), from a lack of copper, iron, manganese or zinc. Too much causes toxicity. Some micronutrients can be applied as seed coatings, and acidifying fertilizers that supply nitrogen keep their cations soluble longer in alkaline soils.

soil-fert-175.title: Potassium, the gatekeeper of a leaf's pores
soil-fert-175.text: Potassium opens and closes a leaf's stomata through an ion pump. It therefore controls water loss from leaves and raises drought tolerance. This primary nutrient is present in all plant parts and activates enzymes of {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and respiration, yet it is built into no major plant constituent. In plant tissue it is outstandingly mobile and soluble. Soils hold 3 to 100 tons of potassium per hectare in the top 20 cm, but only 2 per cent of it is available to plants. Biotite mica and potassium feldspar are common mineral sources, and rhizobacteria help dissolve it with organic acids. Once dissolved, about half is held as exchangeable cations on clay minerals and half stays in the soil solution. As soils dry, potassium can be fixed between the layers of 2:1 clays such as illite, vermiculite and montmorillonite, up to 90 percent within ten minutes. It leaches easily from low-clay soils unless dressings of animal dung or lime offset their poor cation exchange capacity. Potassium-rich soils also yield quality fruit, with better color, shape and sugar content.

soil-fert-159.title: Iron, the metal behind green leaves
soil-fert-159.text: Iron is not part of chlorophyll, yet a plant cannot make chlorophyll without it. This micronutrient is an enzyme cofactor, a helper the enzymes need, in {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and electron transport. Deficiency yellows the tissue between the veins, a form of {{ref:soil-fert-228}}, and causes necrosis. It can stem from excess heavy metals or lime in the soil, or from a lack of copper. Iron(II) is the most useful form because it is more soluble at neutral pH. Plants can also use iron(III) through the photo-reduction of ferric citrate. In the field, iron fertilizer is supplied as a chelate, a compound that holds the metal in a form plants can take up.

soil-fert-228.title: Chlorosis, when green leaves fade to yellow
soil-fert-228.text: A pale leaf belongs to a plant short of food. Chlorosis is the condition in which leaves make too little chlorophyll and turn pale, yellow or yellow-white. Such a plant makes little carbohydrate by {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and may die unless the cause is treated. Causes include soil shortages of iron, magnesium, zinc or nitrogen, a soil pH that locks up minerals, waterlogging and damaged or compacted roots. On French limestone vineyards, grafting vines onto American rootstocks after phylloxera worsened this lime chlorosis. Remedies match the cause: iron chelate or sulfate, magnesium or nitrogen feeds, lime on acid soils and sulfur on alkaline ones.

soil-fert-171.title: Carbon: the nutrient plants pull from the air
soil-fert-171.text: About 45% of a plant's dry mass is carbon, and most of it comes from the air. Plants take carbon mainly as carbon dioxide, through {{ref:soil-hist-147}}. They also take dissolved carbon from the soil solution and receive it through mycorrhizal networks. At its normal 0.03% in air, CO2 can limit growth when water and nutrients are not scarce. Raising CO2 strongly promotes growth, up to levels above 300 ppm. Soil air holds 10 to 100 times the atmospheric concentration. When porosity is low or flooding blocks diffusion, it can reach toxic levels.

soil-fert-229.title: Manganese deficiency and the checkered young leaf
soil-fert-229.text: A four-manganese core drives the oxygen-evolving complex of photosystem II, the heart of {{ref:soil-hist-147}}. That is why most broad-spectrum fertilizers contain manganese. Manganese deficiency is commonest in poorly drained soils and where organic matter is high, and at high pH the metal may be unavailable. Leaves yellow between the veins in a checkered pattern. Young leaves show it first, because manganese is immobile in the plant, unlike magnesium. It is often confused with {{ref:soil-fert-201}}, and the two occur together. Ammonium sulfate lowers pH at once; sulfur works slowly through soil bacteria. The US used about 20,000 tons of manganese fertilizer compounds in 2000.

soil-found-065.title: The oxygen cycle's largest store is rock
soil-found-065.text: Most of Earth's oxygen is locked in stone. By weight, 99.5% sits in the silicate and oxide minerals of the crust and mantle, while air, water and life together hold under 0.05%. The oxygen cycle moves oxygen through the atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and crust. The reactions of {{ref:soil-chem-113}} shift its atoms between oxidation states in ions, oxides and molecules. {{ref:soil-hist-147}} is the main source of free oxygen in the air. Respiration and decay are the main losses, as animals and bacteria consume oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

soil-fert-082.title: Fertilizer burn: when plant food parches a plant
soil-fert-082.text: Fertilizer burn is damage caused by too much fertilizer, the wrong type, or too little water applied with it. Excess salt, nitrogen or ammonia impairs {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and respiration, causing visible burns. When salts outside the root exceed those inside, water stops entering and may even leave the roots, so the plant responds as if in drought. Early signs are white salt marks and crusts around the roots. Later the leaves brown and die, root growth stops and roots may rot. Dry, overheated plants suffer most. Heavy watering washes the salts away; otherwise the roots are cleaned and the plant repotted.

soil-water-113.title: Bringing back the tallgrass prairie
soil-water-113.text: By 1849, settlers had plowed up so much tallgrass prairie that most of its grass species had given way to crops. The soil lost the grasses' extensive fibrous roots. Prairie restoration is the work of returning prairie destroyed by industrial, agricultural, commercial or residential development to its earlier state. It helps conserve topsoil, which is exposed to wind and rain erosion once prairie is plowed under. Prairie grasses also take carbon from the air by {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and store it in the soil, which makes prairie soil useful for locking carbon away. In Europe, former cropland is restored by spontaneous succession, sowing seed mixtures, transferring plant material, and removing and transferring topsoil.

soil-env-102.title: The carbon cycle: one element circling through soil, sea and sky
soil-env-102.text: Limestone cliffs and living cells are built partly of the same element. Carbon is the main component of biological compounds and a major part of many rocks. The carbon cycle is the part of Earth's biogeochemical cycles, described in {{ref:soil-fert-140}}, in which carbon moves among living things, soils, rocks, water and the atmosphere. Scientists divide it into reservoirs: the atmosphere, the land's living things and soils, the ocean, sediments and Earth's interior. Chemical, physical, geological and biological processes shift carbon between them. Near Earth's surface, the ocean holds the largest active store. {{ref:soil-hist-147}} is the main route by which carbon dioxide leaves the air and enters land and ocean life. Left alone, the flows between air, ocean, land and sediments are fairly balanced, so carbon levels would stay roughly stable. Humans have upset that balance for centuries. They changed land use, and they mined and burned coal, petroleum and gas. By 2020 atmospheric carbon dioxide stood nearly 52% above pre-industrial levels, driving global warming. Today the land and the ocean each absorb about one-quarter of human carbon emissions every year.

soil-env-106.title: Soil carbon, a store three times the atmosphere's
soil-env-106.text: Soils hold about 2,700 gigatons (Gt) of carbon, roughly three times as much as the atmosphere. Soil carbon is the solid carbon stored in soils, and it comes in two forms. About 1550 GtC is organic, from plants, animals and microbes, the material of {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Another 950 GtC is inorganic, held in the carbonate minerals met in {{ref:soil-found-034}}. Peat and wetlands hold a further 150 GtC, and surface plant litter 50 GtC. This store is far from idle. About 60 GtC a year accumulates in soil, and an equal 60 GtC a year is respired back to the air. {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, respiration and decomposition set how much carbon stays on land. Soil carbon underpins water holding capacity, nutrient retention and soil structure. It matters for climate too, since soil takes up carbon in the global cycle, and data on it feed global climate models. Those data are inconsistent, with some regions far better covered than others. Human activities have caused a massive loss of soil carbon, yet people could also deliberately return carbon to the soil.

soil-env-212.title: Carbon sequestration: putting carbon away
soil-env-212.text: Turn natural or semi-natural land into cropland, and its soil loses about 30-40% of its organic carbon. Carbon sequestration works in the opposite direction. It is the storing of carbon in a reservoir of the carbon cycle, which limits climate change by reducing carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. It comes in two main types, biological and geological. Biological sequestration, or biosequestration, captures CO2 through living processes such as {{ref:soil-hist-147}}. Land-use and farming changes that speed it up are called carbon farming. Sequestration is sometimes confused with carbon capture and storage, which separates CO2 from industrial sources and stores it underground or under the sea bed. Biological stores can be temporary, because wildfire, disease, economic pressure and politics can release their carbon again. Mineral sequestration is far more durable, locking carbon in insoluble carbonate salts for thousands to millions of years. In soil, carbon keeps changing after land is cleared until a new equilibrium is reached. Leaving residues, using manure and adding perennial crops, with their larger below-ground biomass, all raise carbon input. Outside permafrost, about 70% of the organic carbon in the upper metre lies deeper down, stabilized by its association with minerals.

soil-env-103.title: Two speeds of the carbon cycle
soil-env-103.text: Some carbon turns over in years; some takes millions. The carbon cycle splits into a fast biological cycle and a slow geological one. The fast cycle runs through living things, moving carbon between the atmosphere, land and marine ecosystems, soils and seafloor sediments. It includes annual cycles driven by {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and decadal cycles of vegetation growth and decomposition. The slow cycle runs through rocks. Weathering returns carbon to the atmosphere by degassing and to the ocean by rivers, over spans of millions of years. Between 10 and 100 million tonnes of carbon move around it in a given year.

soil-env-335.title: How soil keeps cycling nutrients and organic matter
soil-env-335.text: The nutrients in soil particles start out locked in crystals. Soil water carrying carbon dioxide slowly dissolves them, a process called {{ref:soil-found-058}}, and releases them into the soil solution, the water held among the particles. Plants then take over. They capture carbon by {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, absorb water and nutrients, and store both in biomass. When plants die or are eaten, organisms decompose the residues and manure, and the nutrients become available again. This loop is the {{ref:soil-fert-146}}. Soil also keeps a reserve. Clays bond with organic molecules, and aggregates shield particles from decomposers. The result is a store of nutrients and energy, richest in the deep-rooted soils of prairie and steppe. Plowing broke the loop. It sped decomposition, so more {{ref:soil-found-045}} was lost than returned, and nutrients left with the crop. Fertilizers later replaced the nutrients, but replacing the lost carbon was mostly ignored. That matters because organic matter forms aggregates that give water storage and gas exchange. Mineral particles and pores give a soil its structure, yet organic matter mostly makes it fertile.

soil-env-365.title: Keeping living roots in the ground all year
soil-env-365.text: Natural forests and prairies are never bare. They keep a continuous plant cover and a litter layer, whereas annual crops leave periods with no living plants, and prairie fallow was shown early on to lower soil organic matter. The practice of continuous living plants tries to close those gaps, mainly by perennializing cropping systems, and it protects soil, diversifies systems and builds soil carbon. The root system explains much of the gain. Plants allocate roughly 40% of net photosynthetic carbon to roots, and perennials give more carbon input than annuals because of larger root systems and a longer {{ref:soil-hist-147}} period. Roots and their microbial communities improve aggregation and hydraulic conductivity. In dry regions they raise porosity and the water retained at field capacity. Longer growth and transpiration from deep in the profile also help reduce salinity, because cover and roots limit evaporation and upward salt movement. Annual systems can approximate it with winter annuals such as winter wheat or fall rye, fall and spring cover crops, relay cropping or intercropping, perennial forages and agroforestry. A {{ref:soil-agri-066}} is the simplest step.

soil-env-222.title: Phytotoxicity: when chemicals stunt or kill plants
soil-env-222.text: Even fertilizer can poison a crop. Phytotoxicity is any harmful effect of a chemical on plant growth, physiology or metabolism. Effects range from disrupted {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, water and nutrient uptake, cell division or germination to stunted growth and death. Over-applied fertilizer salts, urea and the ammonia it releases, and poorly humified compost can all do it. Herbicides harm non-target plants through spray drift or through contaminated straw or manure spread on soil. Metals follow two rules. Co, Cu, Fe, Ni and Zn are needed in trace amounts but turn toxic past a threshold; As, Cd and Pb are toxic at any concentration.

reviews.solute-transport-in-soil: Every contaminant in groundwater is moved by the same few processes. Advection carries it along at the seepage velocity, while molecular drift and dispersion spread it around that path without changing its average speed. Sticking to soil particles alone slows the plume, so less soluble substances can lag hundreds or thousands of times behind the water. Colloids work the other way, letting radionuclides and metals travel farther. The transport equation joins these processes, and models such as Hydrus couple it to the Richards equation, while dye traces test the predictions in the field.
